paragraphs.text: Chapter 2. Exercise
I got really lucky with learning about exercise, and enjoying exercise—but only because I got unlucky first.

Like most kids in my town, I swam and played soccer, but unlike most I got really into skateboarding. I was decent enough at those other activities, but I loved skateboarding best. It felt the most liberating because I could do it any time of day or night, and I loved that there was no official court or playing field—city streets, curbs, benches, and stairs were as varied as they come. And it was transportation too, so it offered all sorts of possibilities for adventure. I could do it alone or with others, and I loved that you could innovate by making up new tricks. The sport was still relatively small at the time (this was the late 1980s and early 1990s) and, as I mentioned in the introduction to this book, several of my friends turned professional just out of high school. Not me. I kept getting hurt. By the time I was a sophomore, I had broken the same foot twice and messed up the arches of my feet.

And that’s how exercise came into my life. Luckily, a supportive physical education teacher named Bob Peters noticed how often I arrived to class on crutches and pointed me toward a small weight room near the pool. No one really used it except the football team, and that was only during the summer months. So in many ways, it was a perfect situation. I could go in there and use the equipment whenever I wanted and I didn’t have to compare my (lack of) strength to anyone else because I was mostly alone. Although I didn’t realize it at the time, the dearth of other people weight training also saved me from the terrible, often dangerous advice people tend to give others in gyms.

The only problem was that I had absolutely no idea what I was doing. There were anatomy charts of muscles and bones and tendons on the walls, and a few diagrams of exercises that were easy enough to follow, but nothing else. That drove me to the library and local bookstore, where I read about weight training. Which left me even more confused. The recommendations were all over the place. “Do one set per body part but super slow.” “Do twenty sets per body part.” “Train for thirty minutes maximum, three times a week.” “Train for two hours, twice a day, six days per week,” and on and on. It was dizzying. I completely empathize with people who experience immense confusion when they try to figure out how best to exercise, because I felt that too.

Luckily (again), one of the books I stumbled upon was by Arthur Jones, the inventor of Nautilus exercise machines. Jones was a proponent of doing short, intense workouts two to three times per week, or even less. While that didn’t sound like enough to get results, I liked that he had a rationale for his suggestions and I liked that his general training philosophy was based on science—in particular the work of physiologist Hans Selye, who studied stress and adaptations to stress. [^1] (More about Selye in the next chapter…)

Exercise, Jones pointed out, is a form of stress that the body adjusts to with both specific adaptations, which reflect the type of stress that had been imposed to create them, and general adaptations, which come from pretty much any physical activity, to varying degrees. [^2] Jones believed the goal of resistance training—or running, or any deliberate exercise for that matter—is the specific adaptations. The general adaptations that also occurred were a welcome bonus. Jones felt that when it came to resistance training, it didn’t take much of the correct type of workout to stimulate the specific adaptations that would lead to, say, getting stronger or increasing the size of a muscle. And those two ideas formed the basis of his program.

I didn’t know if Jones was wrong or right—after all, I had minimal experience with resistance training at that point. I also didn’t have anyone to ask. Besides bodybuilders and football players—of which I was neither—not many people practiced resistance training back then, and most who did either looked big and puffy or veiny and really unnatural, neither of which was my goal. I wanted to get stronger and, at 6′1″ and about 150 pounds, I would not have minded having a bit more muscle too. The photos in Jones’s books featured men and women who looked strong as well as lean. Some were younger, some were older. All that was a stark and welcome contrast to the extreme physiques highlighted in other weight training books and magazines.

And there was more: Jones emphasized that a good exercise program is one that doesn’t take so much time that it disrupts one’s school, work, and relationships. I liked the sound of that too. Hungry to learn more, I tracked down the phone number for one of Jones’s protégés, Mike Mentzer, a legendary bodybuilder turned trainer from the late 1970s and early 1980s. [^3] I called and left a message, and Mike called me back. I was sixteen at the time, and my mother was understandably worried. She wondered: Who was this grown man calling her teenage son at home? Apparently, Mike appreciated that when I called him, I rattled off a quick list of questions onto his answering machine that made it clear I had read Jones’s books. We ended up speaking for several hours over the course of a few months about weight training, fitness more generally, and science—both actual science and scientists. It wasn’t as if he gently took me under his wing though. Mike was super intense. He would sort of bark at me when he spoke, but there was always a hint of kindness in his delivery. And he did charge me $150 for the calls, which was most of my savings at the time but it was well worth it.

I’m telling you this story because what I learned from those calls with Mike has stayed with me and I credit much of my regular progress with resistance training over the last thirty years to him. Here are ten counsels Mike gave me that I never forgot and always strive to implement with respect to resistance training.

• 1 After warming up, do not train for much more than sixty to seventy-five minutes at a time… you’ll progress much faster that way. Occasionally your training may go longer if you are waiting for equipment at a gym, but that’s just about the only reason to extend a session much beyond seventy-five minutes.
• 2 Always strive to use good form, meaning use a full range of motion for every repetition of every set, and control the weight from start to finish.

• 3 Learn to use resistance as a tool to stress the muscles you’re trying to train. Focus as you do the lift to feel the muscles you’re trying to train working. Mike added: If you can’t feel the muscle you’re trying to target you’ll want to use “pre-exhaustion” techniques when you train. I explain what pre-exhaustion is later, but as the name suggests, it involves doing an isolation exercise (where only one joint moves) immediately before you do a compound exercise (where multiple joints move) for the same muscle. Mike knew most people hate doing pre-exhaustion exercises because they require using less weight on the compound movement. But for getting results with otherwise hard-to-feel and slow-to-progress muscles, he was spot on.

• 4 If you’re new to resistance training, you’ll benefit greatly by taking one to three weeks to find the right movements that collectively allow you to target all the major muscles of your body and that work best for your body mechanics. Learn to execute those movements correctly using relatively light (for you) weights, meaning an amount of resistance where you can do ten to twelve repetitions, even though you could easily do five more. This one-to-three-week “break-in” period is about learning how to train before you start the real work. If you’ve been regularly training with weights for a while, I suggest you take a full week off. Stay out of the gym completely for seven, or even up to ten, days. You may feel like you’re standing still during this period but it’s critical to your long-term progress, and you’ll thank me later. Once you start your real workouts, it doesn’t take many sets per muscle group to get the results you want, IF you do them with proper form… and intensity.

• 5 Intensity is defined as working with a weight that is heavy enough (for you) that it limits you to completing six to twelve repetitions maximum in good form. There are times to deliberately use heavier weights that limit you to three to five repetitions maximum, or lighter weights that permit you to do thirteen to twenty repetitions maximum. When and where to do that comes later. If you’re not familiar with any of these terms, don’t worry. I’ll get into all this as the chapter unfolds. But what struck me looking back on these notes as I wrote this chapter is how many sets and exercises to do, and how often to train, was debated like crazy back then and it still is now. Mike was a bit extreme; he favored doing very few actual work sets of an exercise—meaning effortful sets, not warm-ups. In fact, he suggested doing even just one work set per exercise, and one to two exercises per muscle group. I will address the science-supported and practical reasons for doing a bit more than that later. But for now, let’s take in Mike’s points about a relatively low number of work sets, or what is referred to as a volume of sets. Because one thing most everyone agrees on now that Mike extolled is this: If done properly, you don’t need a high volume of sets per exercise or muscle group, and that more is often counterproductive. And so we continue, with more from Mike.

• 6 Train three times per week but know that your body gets stronger on the rest days in between training sessions, and mostly while you sleep. Hard training taxes your whole nervous system, too, not just the muscles and tendons and ligaments you trained, so to make the best progress, every twelve to sixteen weeks, or even every ten to twelve weeks, take one complete week off from resistance training to allow your muscles and nervous system to recover. You’ll likely make much more progress in the long run.

• 7 Your body adapts to training. Making progress requires continually stressing your muscles by increasing the amount of weight you use for exercise over time. You can also do more repetitions with the same amount of weight, but once you can do ten to twelve repetitions with a given weight on a given exercise, using proper form, you need to increase the amount of weight in order to continue to make progress. That is because to grow in strength and size, a muscle must be stressed to its limit. This is known as progressive overload. To ensure you’re doing this, take notes on the number of sets and repetitions you’re doing for each workout, along with the weights you’re using. This is the best way to make sure you’re progressively overloading your muscles from one workout to the next.

• 8 Take each work set to failure, the point where you can’t move the weight anymore in good form despite your absolute greatest effort. And sometimes you have to push past failure by getting assistance from a training partner who nudges the weight just a bit, or by immediately reducing the weight and doing two to three more repetitions until you hit failure again.
• 9 Learn to enjoy training hard. Don’t socialize in the gym. Warm up, train, and get out! And undoubtedly the best and most classic Mentzer-ism of all:
• 10 “DO NOT LISTEN TO WHAT ANYONE ELSE TELLS YOU AS MOST PEOPLE WHO LIFT WEIGHTS ARE MORONS AND MOST OF WHAT THEY DO AND SAY IS TOTAL BS!”

(Mike literally yelled number 10 into the phone so loud that I winced and had to move the receiver away from my ear. Later I understood what words of wisdom and care those were. To be fair, there are many folks in the fitness education and training community who offer great advice, but Mike wasn’t terribly off with this one.)

However coarse the delivery, those ten points were (and remain) gems that we can all benefit from. Again, as I said, I got lucky. We now have tons of peer-reviewed science to support the general logic of Mike’s advice, although at the time, much of it ran countercurrent to the dominant views about resistance training, most notably the popular idea at the time that “more volume is better.” As it turns out, quality reps and sets are what count, and it does not take much high-quality resistance training to trigger the specific adaptations Jones outlined in his book. (Note: Quality has many meanings, which we will cover repeatedly below.)

Of course, those ten points do not exhaustively cover all one needs to know about resistance training, and considering the results of studies that have been done since, there are some important caveats that I’ll address. What I can say, however, is that I took Mike’s general advice to heart.

After our first call, I took a full week off from any resistance training and then, even though I had been lifting for about six months, I devoted a few weeks to finding the free-weight, weight-machine, and body-weight-only exercises that worked best for me—meaning the ones I could do for full range of motion, pain free, and that allowed me to stress each of the major muscle groups. I found the right combination of compound (multi-joint) exercises and isolation (single-joint) exercises for each muscle group, like the shoulders, biceps, quadriceps, et cetera.

Then I started doing resistance training three times per week, training different muscles on each of those three days: calves and legs one day, then a day or two off, then chest, back, and abdominals (and neck), then a day off, then shoulders and arms, another day off, and then back to calves and legs day. So again, three days total in the gym per week. I’ve done that body part–split pretty much consistently for thirty-five years now. Even if I am traveling, I find a gym to do these workouts. And if I go to a location where I can’t find a gym, I’ll do body-weight-only exercises, or I take the week off and stay active in other ways. While general activity is no substitute for resistance training, I have found that a week off approximately every four months can be beneficial. I can arrange it to happen during a vacation or other travel, or if I get sick—fortunately a rarity for me—I don’t train. I rest up and stay out of the gym (and thus avoid getting others sick too!) and that becomes the week off. Approaching resistance training this way has allowed me to make consistent progress with about three hours per week of resistance training while still fully enjoying other aspects of life and avoiding injuries.

Before going any further I want to acknowledge something that Mike got somewhat wrong and that is important to highlight here. There is not one best way to resistance train! You won’t find too many effective programs that recommend fewer than three days of resistance training per week, but there are some good ones that involve more days. Some programs, like the one described in this book, are based on a body part split in which you train different body parts on different days. And even those splits can vary. For instance some people like to train all their pushing muscles of the upper body (chest, shoulders, triceps) on one day, and pulling muscles (back and biceps) on another day, and then legs a different day. Other programs have you train your whole body in every workout; others still alternate between upper and lower body workouts. All these can work. Below I explain the rationale for the split I use and suggest—because it offers some not-so-obvious benefits. The point stands, nonetheless, that there are a lot of ways to resistance train.

Yet there is a core set of principles upon which all people—women, men, inexperienced, experienced, young, old—must rely on to build an effective program. I define an “effective program” as one that people are likely to stick to over many years, and that works well for those also doing cardiovascular exercise, which we know is also vital to our health and provides distinct benefits from resistance training. Many people want to grow certain muscles and leave others as they are. Others want to grow all their muscles. An effective program should offer all those options too.

It also means a program that does not sap your energy but instead gives you more energy. After all, what good is a program that leaves you tired and hungry to an extent that inhibits your work and relationships? While it is normal (and reflective of an effective workout) to be tired after a training session, that fatigue should be somewhat transient, even that day. Your workout shouldn’t leave you dragging. During your work sets, you work hard—both mentally and physically—and you’ll sweat and perhaps get a bit sore, but those are not the goal. Those are the by-products of quality workouts. You also want to still be able to think and walk (!) in the hours and days that follow.

I’ve come up with a template to help everyone. It’s part of why I call it a foundational fitness program—so named because it’s grounded in research, the ideas above and that follow below, and the core physiological principles that undergird all effective programs. These principles will never change because they reflect the mechanisms by which muscles, bones, and connective tissues get stronger and, if desired, grow larger. If you make sure that your resistance training follows this template, you can still tailor it to your goals, body type, schedule, and the phase of life you are in. That’s what I mean by a foundational fitness program.

You might be thinking, “What about cardiovascular training?” There too I got really lucky. By the time I was seventeen, I was doing resistance training three times per week per Mike’s instructions. I got great results in terms of strength and muscle size increases. And I enjoyed it. But I quickly found that I missed outdoor activities. Mike subscribed to the common idea back then that you couldn’t make meaningful progress with resistance training while also doing endurance-type activities, like running or biking. The reverse was also thought to be true. Nonetheless, I disobeyed Mike and what all other training books at the time said and I started running on the days that I didn’t resistance train. I had an excellent reason to. My girlfriend lived about fifteen minutes away by car, I didn’t have my own car yet, there was no bus to her house, and Uber didn’t exist back then. So, much of the time I would just run to her house, which took me about forty-five to sixty minutes, thanks to all the hills. Sometimes I would bike there instead, which took about thirty minutes. Once again, I had no idea what I was doing. I would just set out and go. Ah, the joys of being young and naïve. And in love.

Here’s where I got lucky: I was surprised at what happened. Instead of getting weaker, which is what everyone said would happen, I got stronger. And instead of resistance training making me slower at running and biking, which is what our school’s cross-country coach told me would happen, I found I could run and bike faster and farther, and without any pain.

I also noticed that I always felt better mentally when I did a mix of cardiovascular and resistance training across the week, as opposed to just one or the other. I thought perhaps it was the fresh air… but I noticed this even if it was raining and I was forced to run on a treadmill.

I should mention that this was the early 1990s, and the ideologies within different sports and sectors of the fitness world were still very siloed. Today, we believe that being stronger helps in pretty much every sport and physical activity. Back then people also thought that if you did resistance training and then stopped, your muscles would turn to fat. Today we know that is false—in fact, it’s impossible. Nowadays, most every serious athlete resistance trains during both the main and the offseason. And we now know that even if you don’t play a sport, if your goal is to be healthy and fit, and to stay uninjured, and live as long as possible, and to do so with vigor, you’re best off doing a combination of both resistance training and cardiovascular training. This is true for women and for men. We also know that what defines an effective resistance training program is the same for women and men, such as the need for intensity—training to failure on work sets (or close to failure)—as well as proper form, allowing sufficient rest between workouts for specific adaptations to occur, and more. As Lauren Colenso-Semple, a PhD in integrative physiology and a strength and conditioning coach, and one of the world’s leading experts in strength and hypertrophy training, stated so clearly (and adamantly) when she was a guest on my podcast, all the data point to the fact that when it comes to resistance training to improve strength and/or muscle size, the same principles and techniques apply to women and to men—including the need to train to failure or very close to it. [^4] Looking back, for me it was thanks to those repeated foot injuries from skateboarding, the generosity of a physical education teacher, a few good books, some formative calls with one of the world’s experts in resistance training, and being a naïve, lovestruck teenager that I learned early on how to get in and stay in great all-around shape. Lucky indeed.

And I promise you: If you follow the template here and add in cardiovascular training, too, you can get into and stay in great all-around shape at any age. Yes, nutrition matters but making exercise part of your life will absolutely make you a much healthier person, mentally and physically.
In this chapter I teach you how to do that. And if you already have a fitness program, I’m confident you’ll still glean a ton of new knowledge that you can use from these pages.

Most people exercise because they want to feel and look good in their body. They also want longevity—not just to live as long as possible, but to be capable of doing any number of practical things without pain and, ideally, with relative ease. For example, having enough endurance for a long hike with a backpack. Being strong enough to lift boxes of books or help move furniture. Fast enough to sprint for (and catch) a plane or train without tearing a muscle. Able to open a jar when asked. The protocols here will enable you to do all that. They will also help you achieve the body composition (i.e., lean tissue-to-fat ratio) you want, while still allowing you to eat well, and feel more vital. Exercise is extremely potent medicine and, as with sleep, it’s one of the best investments you can make toward your mental and physical health. The benefits start from the minute you begin each workout.

If all this gives the impression I love exercise… I do, on some days. Training is definitely a pleasure for me, especially if I’ve slept well, I’m hydrated, I’m caffeinated, and if there’s no big stressor weighing on me. That’s a lot of ifs, so it won’t surprise you that those conditions are often hard to achieve because, well, life happens. I too sometimes get less-than-optimal sleep. I too have a full schedule. I too experience stress. I’ve had lapses due to the occasional cold. It happens to all of us.

That said, really understanding how exercise works and how much good can come from a few hours a week of focused training can keep us on the journey to get and stay fit when we are not feeling motivated. I look forward to workouts because I know that the way I’m training works. That is priceless. Especially for people who don’t like exercise, but like the feeling of having done it, knowing your time was well spent—that it will get you results—is a game changer. In fact, a really good program of the sort I describe here can allow you to make progress most every single week.

I mentioned earlier in this introduction that I empathize with people who experience immense confusion when they try to figure out how best to exercise, because I felt that too. So perhaps you’re wondering: Why not just discuss “the best way to exercise” here? Maybe you’re sensing a pattern: Just like there’s no “best” way to resistance train, there’s no best way to exercise. We know that resistance training is key. So is doing cardiovascular training. And we need mobility and some degree of flexibility too. There are literally thousands of different programs for each of these. But, if you understand the principles by which different types of exercise benefit us in different ways, you can come up with the truly best exercise program for you. As Andy Galpin, PhD, an expert in exercise physiology, shared with me on my podcast, “The methods are many, the principles are few.” [^5] Meaning there are many different ways to go about generating specific adaptations like strength and muscle size increases, or improved heart stroke volume, which is the amount of blood your heart pumps. That’s the power of understanding how the brain and body work, and that’s why I explain the mechanisms behind each protocol.

I should say, too, that these principles are broad—I don’t talk about specific demographics here. These are written to help the widest possible audience of women and men of any age. Know that I don’t lump those two groups together casually. As mentioned above, the science shows that the principles of an effective exercise program are the same for men and for women. Of course, if ever the science points to key differences, I highlight them. But again, if you understand the mechanisms behind a protocol, you can personalize it for your specific needs. Likewise, if you are training for performance in a sport, you might adjust these, again, as you see fit.
What is exercise?

Peering into the history of exercise turns out to be both interesting and informative. And helpful, when it comes to our health goals. [^6] An Indian physician named Susruta, who lived around 600 BCE, was one of the first known practitioners to prescribe exercise. “It should be taken every day,” he wrote. “Diseases fly from the presence of a person habituated to regular physical exercise.” Susruta’s words are as relevant today as they were during his lifetime.

The problem is how to implement the prescription. Many people don’t do it, or they do it wrong and end up discouraged, injured, or both. So many times I hear people say, “I used to work out every day,” or “I used to be so fit,” or “I don’t have the time or energy to exercise anymore.” What is rarely discussed is that exercise, done correctly, gives you energy. It extends your life (i.e., gives you more time). It also increases your level of focus for many hours afterward, which also saves you time. And there’s more. Research shows that regular exercise can be as or even more effective for improving mood and lowering anxiety than prescription antidepressants or talk therapy. [^7] On, and on, and on. Exercise is not a cure-all, but it is often a way to address many of the physical and mental health issues people struggle with. It’s just that, as a species, we have not quite come to understand how potent a medicine exercise really is.

Then there are those who exercise consistently but overdo one type or just focus on their favorite sport, like running or tennis, Pilates or spin class, and miss out on the very real health benefits that come from variety.
In my experience, very few people know how to get in great all-around shape properly. Even fewer stay there. The good news is that doing so is pretty simple, again, once you know how.

It comes in three basic varieties: resistance training, cardiovascular exercise, and mobility and/or flexibility. Resistance exercise is where you use some weight—your body weight, weight machines, or free weights—to challenge your neuromuscular system and connective tissues. Resistance training also strengthens your bones. The hallmark of classic cardiovascular exercise is an increased heart rate for at least twelve minutes and up to seventy-five minutes—or in some cases even longer. There are arguments to be made that one can get effective cardiovascular workouts in shorter bouts of activity, through what’s often called high-intensity interval training (HIIT). But we will return to that nuance later. Finally, mobility and flexibility challenges our ability to stably shift between different bodily positions, and to have access to a full range of functional motion if we need it for athletics or simply in everyday life. If you’re now thinking “So I have to do three types of exercise? I barely have time for one!” don’t despair. Although it can be great to have mobility and flexibility practice, as I describe later in this chapter, you can see meaningful benefits from protocols that take very little time to complete, in one case just five minutes. And the resistance and cardiovascular sessions I describe below are aimed to give you the maximum benefits for time spent.
What is the goal of exercise?

Believe it or not, the most important thing to understand about exercise is why you’re doing it. I don’t mean your psychology here. I am referring to what you are trying to achieve with each workout; why you are doing specifically what you are doing. It ensures every workout leads you to achieve your goals. For all that has been written and said about exercise, it often misses this crucial point. All effective forms of exercise share a common purpose: to trigger a set of specific and general adaptations in your body and brain.

Exercise is the stimulus, and the general and specific adaptations are your body’s response to the stimulus. Exercise can also drive aesthetic changes, like fat loss, or improve sports performance, but those are secondary. “Wait!” I hear you saying, “I exercise to stay fit. Just tell me how to do that.” I will, but I promise you will accomplish your goals much faster, and you will make consistent progress, if you understand exercise in this stimulus-adaptation context.

Here’s an example of how specific adaptations work. Let’s say you run or cycle at a moderate pace for thirty minutes. I’m talking about a pace where you can barely hold a conversation without gasping for air. While you do this your heart rate and blood pressure will rise substantially, you’ll breathe more rapidly, you’ll sweat, your muscles probably will burn a bit, and your immune system will release a bunch of pro-inflammatory molecules such as interleukin-6 into your blood. [^8] Sounds terrible, right? Wrong. This constellation of responses—what we call the exercise-induced stress response—will lead to a set of adaptations that directly reflect the stress you just experienced but in the opposite direction. Thousands of coordinated, metabolic, molecular and even genetic changes occur when we exercise—a “molecular choreography,” as one group of researchers has put it. [^9]
After doing this for some time, your resting heart rate, blood pressure, and circulating levels of inflammatory molecules will be lower than they were before you set out on that run.

When most people think about what they accomplished by exercising, they tend to think about the calories burned or the mood enhancement it provides in the hours that follow. That’s all well and good, but the real magic of exercise resides in the specific and general adaptations it produces. Those are the real “gains” of exercise. They last for days and they compound over time. They literally change your body and brain, and do so in ways that reflect the stress you experienced during the workout. That makes you a physiologically different person—capable of more in every area of life related to the exercise-induced adaptations—stronger, and faster, with more vigor and endurance, and more capable all around. Once you understand and experience the stimulus-adaptation process, you come to understand what effective effort is and when to rest to glean the adaptations you worked to trigger. It can make you wiser too. In fact, as we will cover later in chapter 6—neuroplasticity, or your ability to learn and rewire your brain—follows the same general contour of “failures” (from genuine efforts to do something!) prompted by specific adaptations that will help you overcome those “failures” in the near future.

The effects of quality exercise on your ability to learn extend way beyond just metaphor. Exercise can directly facilitate neuroplasticity by allowing it to occur. [^10] Like heat makes metal pliable, so too exercise brings the brain into a state where new neural connections in the brain and body can be forged. [^11] Take for instance a 2011 study by a group of psychologists at the University of Pittsburgh. They randomized 120 older adults (average age sixty-seven) into two groups: one to cardiovascular exercise, the other to stretching only. The cardiovascular exercise group walked for increasing durations of time, reaching a maximum of forty minutes per session by week seven. By that point, the walking was brisk enough to get the participants’ heart rates up to 50 to 60 percent of their maximum. And they did three sessions per week. The participants continued with that regimen for a year. According to the results, the hippocampus—a brain region associated with learning and memory—increased in volume by about 2 percent among the cardiovascular group, whereas it shrank by about 1.4 percent among the stretching-only group. While that might not seem like a lot, these findings are noteworthy because a shrinking hippocampus is linked to memory impairments during the later decades of life. A rather simple low-intensity exercise intervention seems to not only prevent brain deterioration but also trigger brain growth. Other studies, including those exploring higher-intensity exercise and resistance training show similar—and in some cases greater—neuroplasticity brought about by exercise. [^12]

It perhaps shouldn’t surprise us that exercise can open the gates for learning in the brain. A disproportionate amount of our brain’s volume is devoted to generating our movements. Rodolfo Llinás, MD, PhD, a neuroscientist at NYU School of Medicine, cites an odd but telling example of the sea squirt, a spineless marine creature. [^13] Young sea squirts swim freely until they are fully grown. The adults then stick themselves onto a rock and become filter feeders, catching whatever happens to float by. When this transition from swimming to sedentary occurs, sea squirts eat their own brains, leaving only what is necessary for their new passive style of feeding. Llinás’s story about a distantly related animal is relevant to us for two reasons. First, it provides a warning to humans with an overly sedentary lifestyle. As humans age and become less mobile, their brains degenerate too, albeit not as dramatically as does the sea squirt brain. [^14] Second, people who continue to exercise—in particular those who do exercise that is challenging (but safe) for them, offset much of typical age-related brain loss that is otherwise observed. This has real implications, allowing them to maintain youthful cognitive function well into their later years, possibly through neurogenesis, the addition of new brain neurons. [^15] Deliberate, repetitive, effortful movements that elicit the short-term stress responses (discussed throughout this chapter) trigger a battery of chemical and neural feedback signals to the brain, which both supports the existing brain cells and the connections we would otherwise lose over time, as well as releases signals that cause neurons to grow new connections. This makes sense if you think about the sea squirt anecdote once more. Our brain is the most metabolically demanding organ in our body. Much of that organ is devoted to our ability to generate movement. [^16] If we don’t move, much of our brain is less active too. Am I telling you that we must exercise just to maintain the brain capacity we have? Indeed I am. Exercise—provided it is of sufficient intensity—makes us cognitively resilient.

The benefits of exercise to brain health and neuroplasticity turn out to be robust at every age, for women, for men, for people vulnerable to age-related cognitive decline, and for both neurologically healthy and unhealthy people alike. Resistance training and cardiovascular training both impart huge benefits, but their combination (typically in separate workouts) turns out to be the most effective stimulus for brain health and neuroplasticity. [^17] And when mobility and flexibility, and walking, are added in, the positive results increase significantly.

Some of the effects of exercise on brain health and neuroplasticity are the result of something called brain-derived neurotrophic factor, or BDNF, a protein our brain makes that can exert a powerful role on learning and memory by virtue of its ability to sculpt and reinforce new neural circuit connections. [^18] Numerous studies have found that exercise leads to elevated levels of BDNF in the brain. [^19] These elevations are temporary, [^20] but enough to open the window for neuroplasticity for several hours after the exercise has ceased. Exercise also increases the release of catecholamines: [^21] that dopamine, epinephrine, norepinephrine trio that we discussed in the chapter on sleep and that we will revisit throughout this book. When that trio is deployed in the body and brain, our levels of alertness and focus are increased, allowing us to access the memories, skills, and cognitive abilities we harbor in our neural circuits. As neuromodulators, the catecholamines also can open the opportunity for neuroplasticity. (I explain this process in more detail in chapter 6.)

The way to think about the effects of exercise on brain health and neuroplasticity, therefore, is that moderate-to-intense exercise reinforces and maintains the brain functions we already have and lets us access the best of our attentional systems for focus and memory. It also opens the window for you to learn at an accelerated rate after the exercise session. Exercise alone won’t make you smarter, but it opens the door for you to become smarter, should you decide to put in the effort to do so. (Chapter 6 explains the best and fastest way to do that.)

It’s important to remember that any learning facilitated by elevated levels of BDNF is not confined to the neural circuits involved in the exercise that triggered it. Rather, BDNF will facilitate whatever learning we pursue while its levels are elevated. As one of many examples, just six minutes of intense running improved the ability of twenty-seven healthy adults to learn new words. [^22] The improvements in learning and retention were tied to elevated levels of BDNF, along with elevated catecholamines: dopamine and epinephrine. Moderate-to-high-intensity exercise is arguably the best type of workout to trigger this process. People will debate whether resistance training is as effective at increasing neuroplasticity as cardiovascular training is. The key variable seems to be the intensity of training; it has to be sufficiently high. When done correctly, resistance training can be at least as taxing as intense cardiovascular training when viewed through the lens of neurological demand, and perhaps more. [^23]

Another way that exercise supports our brain and body is that it markedly improves sleep quality and duration. [^24] Remember from chapter 1: Morning workouts appear to shorten the amount of time it takes to fall asleep at night, and regular exercise has been found to improve the overall quality of sleep for adults. In a study including forty-eight adults with insomnia, moderate aerobic exercise improved sleep, and helped the participants feel less stressed. [^25]

One caveat. If exercise is very intense and done too close to your desired bedtime, it can be detrimental to sleep. (We cover this more in chapter 1 and chapter 3.) It’s best to either avoid intense exercise in the hours prior to sleep, or if you can’t, to make sure you engage in some deliberate downregulation practices, such as a few minutes of long-exhale breathing or a hot shower, so that it does not negatively impact your sleep.

There are many reasons why appropriately timed exercise improves sleep. As discussed in chapter 1, the chemical adenosine, which not only builds up in the brain and body throughout the day but is also further increased with exercise, creates an increasing pressure to sleep. [^26] So exercise helps promote great sleep and reduces factors that lead to poor sleep. Regular physical activity also appears to increase the amount of time we spend in restorative slow-wave deep sleep, regardless of what time of day we exercise, and that translates to us feeling more rested when we wake. [^27]

Then there is the benefit of moderate to intense exercise on our subjective waking experience, specifically on our feelings of well-being. Although “well-being” might sound nonscientific, for a lot of people it’s an important barometer they use to gauge their quality of life. People who don’t like exercise often look at me askance when I say that exercise improves mood, and not just because it helps us sleep better. But it’s true: Exercise makes us happy. [^28] And relaxed. [^29] A moderate to intense workout is a proven, excellent way to snap ourselves out of a slump. [^30] Exercise reduces our baseline levels of stress, [^31] increases our capacity to show resilience in a wide range of circumstances, [^32] and reduces anger. [^33] These mood enhancements of exercise come from several different chemicals: dopamine, which increases motivation, focus, energy, and cognitive function; [^34] and serotonin, which does many things, including help make us more resistant to challenges.

And here’s a fun fact: The lactate your body produces during high-intensity exercise can physically modify—or lactylate—proteins in the brain, altering how neurons communicate. A recent study found that lactate production spurred by exercise reduced anxiety-related behaviors in mice, apparently by supporting the molecular machinery present at synapses between neurons in the prefrontal cortex. [^35] The prefrontal cortex has many parts and functions, but will come up repeatedly in this book in the context of reducing impulsivity, decreasing anxiety, and learning new information and skills. [^36]

There’s more. Exercise has a surprising effect on our energy levels. The relationship between exercise and energy is key to understand, especially for those who feel they don’t have the energy to exercise. After all, exercise requires energy, right? Right. For those who don’t enjoy it or who have a ton of demands on their schedule and may not be sleeping well or enough, that’s especially true. Add in a bit of low-level or major depression, anxiety about finances or the state of the world, or challenges with relationships in your life and, voila: You have a person who quite understandably does not want to exercise, and very likely won’t exercise, no matter how many studies about its benefits or inspirational tales they see and hear. If this is you or someone you know, I hope what I’m about to share will help.

Yes, exercise requires energy to initiate and to complete, but it also gives us energy. I’m not just referring to energy in the psychological sense. I mean it gives us actual chemical energy and it does so by changing the electrical state of your nervous system. Work from neuroscientist Peter Strick’s laboratory, at the University of Pittsburgh, identified three sets of brain areas that, when activated, communicate with our adrenal glands to cause them to release adrenaline. [^37] In turn, this adrenaline activates receptors on our vagus nerve, which is a dense neural pathway that bidirectionally connects our body and brain. Our vagus nerve then triggers the release of norepinephrine from the locus coeruleus, which in turn can increase release of dopamine, acetylcholine, and other neuromodulators in other brain centers. [^38] Other research found that exercise enhances a group of neurons in the hypothalamus—known as VMH SF1 neurons—whose activity is required in order for endurance-specific adaptations to occur. [^39] Meaning, the brain is what actually coordinates the specific bodily adaptations that effective exercise triggers. Put differently, your body changes because your brain tells it to.

While the abilities of our brain to energize and change our body are incredible, the key practical questions are: “What are the magical brain areas that, when made active, flick the first domino in this brain–adrenals–vagus–locus coeruleus/basal ganglia circuit? And how do we activate those brain areas?” The answer, Strick found, is a set of brain regions that control voluntary movement of the major muscles of the limbs—and the core muscles; yes, your abdominals, or abs, but also the sheets of muscles below and all around them, such as the rectus abdominis and obliques. Translation: Deliberate movement of your limbs and your core muscles creates chemical energy that activates your brain to want to further move your body, and gives you heightened levels of motivation to continue doing so.

We can use that exercise-induced energy not just to exercise more or harder. It can be directed toward cognitive activities in the hours after you exercise or simply to go about the tasks of your day with more motivation and focus. Provided we don’t exercise to the point of exhaustion, exercise markedly improves our brain function, psychological state, and overall energy levels. Yes, it involves hormones. Yes, it involves endorphins (everyone seems to know this based on the notion of a “runner’s high”). But it also involves a shift in brain state.

And exercise affects more than just our brain. There’s perhaps the most familiar benefit: our heart health. In 1986 researchers from Stanford and Harvard reported their findings from sixteen years of tracking physical activity and the causes of death of nearly seventeen thousand people between the ages of thirty-five and seventy-four. [^40] They found that the more a person walked, climbed stairs, or played sports, the less likely they were to die of heart disease. And the correlation was linear: The more physically active someone was, the lower the risk. This connection existed regardless of smoking status, weight, or having a parent who’d died young (a potential indicator of an inherited condition). The report, led by noted epidemiologist Ralph Paffenbarger, MD, and published in the New England Journal of Medicine, was considered a landmark—proof that exercise improved longevity, largely by preventing cardiovascular illnesses.

Research since confirms this finding. In one study, researchers followed 3,307 people with heart disease from 1985 to 2014. [^41] Everyone in the study had been encouraged to exercise and lose weight. After thirty years, the researchers could see that while weight loss alone did not reduce the risk of death, exercise did. Other data confirm exercise’s significance, even when people have other risk factors. One group of researchers described this link starkly, back in 1996. [^42] “Low fitness is an important precursor of mortality,” they wrote. To put that in plain language: People who aren’t active are more likely to die young.

One mechanism behind this link is increased insulin sensitivity. [^43] Insulin is a hormone made and released from your pancreas that is essential for keeping your blood sugar, or glucose, levels within a particular range. Almost every cell in the body, including our neurons, requires glucose to function. Glucose comes from the food we eat and stored sources of energy, such as glycogen in our muscles and liver and adipose tissue, what is commonly referred to as body fat. Resistance to insulin leads to a buildup of glucose in our blood, which damages the endothelial cells that make up our capillaries, veins, and arteries, and deprives all cells of the glucose they need, impairing their functioning. It thus can cause cardiovascular disease and cerebrovascular diseases such as stroke and dementia. Exercise increases insulin sensitivity and can even improve the expression of genes that regulate insulin and glucose over long time spans which means more stable energy levels and reduced cellular inflammation and other symptoms of metabolic disorders. [^44] People with diabetes are more sensitive to insulin after exercising, [^45] too, and nondiabetics derive additional benefits from exercise-induced insulin sensitivity. Such benefits can be seen even after just one moderate workout.
What’s more, exercise can make your muscles become much better at pulling glucose out of the bloodstream, which ultimately helps your body handle carbohydrates more efficiently. [^46]

Finally (although I could go on!), there’s this: As you now know from everything you’ve just read, exercise can make you healthier and happier, and it can allow you to get smarter too. It will also extend your life.

One analysis examined data from thirteen studies that directly compared life expectancy among active and inactive people. [^47] Eight of those studies included both men and women, and the results showed an average increase of 3.7 years of life among people who exercised regularly compared to those who did not. While it’s great to have a physically active job or lifestyle, the benefits of structured exercise are independent. You need both of these in your life.

And you don’t need to have been a longtime fitness devotee either. A Swedish study of 2,205 middle-aged men found that people who started to exercise between the ages of fifty and sixty experienced the same life-extending benefit as men who’d been working out all their lives and continued to do so as they got older. [^48] There are also now studies of people who started resistance training in their mid-sixties, seventies, and even eighties, and all made excellent progress in strength and derived many other general health and lifestyle benefits. In fact, the group in their eighties made the same degree of progress in muscle mass and strength compared to people who had been exercising regularly for decades! [^49]

There is a lot more to say about exercise and longevity, but the effects are multifaceted. Some of them arrive via improved metabolic health and fuel utilization. Some via improved sleep, and improved immune system functioning—again, assuming we don’t chronically exhaust ourselves with over-exercising. The point is: Exercise gives us life—literally.
So by now I hope you’re on board with the “why.” We can move on to the “how.”
How should I exercise?

As I’ve mentioned, there is no one best way to exercise but there is, I believe, a best way to structure an effective exercise program. It starts with setting a foundation that you can build on—not necessarily by adding more sessions but by changing the type and amount of exercise, and the sequence in which you do them each week. Let me show you how.

The data point to everyone—men and women, young and old—needing sessions specifically to maintain or build muscle and strength, as well as sessions to keep or improve cardiovascular fitness. Also, mobility and flexibility aren’t just nice to have, they are crucial to ensure we can exercise for the rest of our lives relatively pain free, and just as importantly, to live full lives by virtue of the number and types of activities we can partake in. Sports, recreation, playing with our kids or grandkids, and even household chores require some degree of mobility and flexibility.

The five protocols that follow have everything you need to build an effective exercise program that can be customized for your age, fitness and aesthetic goals, and schedule. It makes the puzzle pieces I’ve outlined above fit together. They include the foundational fitness program I discussed: three days of resistance training—all relatively brief but intense workouts—and three days of cardio—each of different duration and intensity, and done on non-resistance training days. Plus daily walking that can be worked into your existing daily activities and some mobility and flexibility exercises that are fast, yet also effective. It is designed to be compatible with your life.

Yes, maintaining a consistent routine will require some commitment, even when a workout is the last thing you want to do. But remember: You will never feel worse for having exercised. And completing a workout is much easier than you might think, if you keep in mind that all effective exercise is stress designed to create specific and general adaptations. Collectively, these are certain to make you more fit and healthy and capable than you ever imagined.
EXERCISE PROTOCOL 1 Walk as Much as Possible Each Day
WHAT TO DO
• Incorporate walking into your daily life. Also, in these instances in particular, if you can: Walk for five to ten minutes after meals, when health benefits of this activity are amplified.
• Walk or pace for at least five minutes for every thirty minutes of sitting or standing.

• Consider a walk-and-work desk. If you need to be at a desk for work for long stretches of time, a sit-stand desk may be a good investment. Even better is a walk-and-work desk, with a treadmill that fits below.
• Seven thousand steps per day is a good goal, and ten thousand is even better. Accelerometers, step counters, or even your phone can help you keep track, but are not necessary.
HOW IT WORKS

This isn’t that foundational fitness program I discussed; it’s something even more essential. While walking isn’t the only exercise we need to do, it’s listed as the first protocol in this section because it should not be thought of as an add-on. Rather, it is at the bedrock of a healthy lifestyle, just as viewing morning sunlight is the basis of a good sleep routine. Simply walking for at least an hour a day (total, not even all at once) is one of the best things you can do to protect yourself against illness and improve your overall health. The data show us why.

A group of researchers from across the US recruited 2,110 people between the ages of thirty-eight and fifty years to wear an accelerometer, or a step counter, for one year. [^50] The researchers then collected health data on these individuals for the next ten years (on average). Their analysis, published in JAMA Network Open in 2021, showed that people who took at least seven thousand steps per day during the decade of the study had a significantly lower mortality risk compared to people who took fewer steps.

In 2023, researchers from Kyoto University, in Japan, and UCLA published their study of 3,101 adults who took eight thousand steps three to seven days per week, eight thousand steps one to two days per week, or fewer than eight thousand steps on any one day in their week. [^51] Health data were collected over the ten years following study enrollment. Like the earlier report, this one found that taking eight thousand steps or more correlated with a significantly lower risk of death from all causes, including heart disease. The benefit appeared to plateau at three to four days per week of eight thousand steps.

And walking protects against more than heart disease. Researchers from Denmark and Australia investigated the link between walking and dementia risk. [^52] They monitored 78,340 adults for an average of seven years and, like the studies above, saw a link between walking and a lower risk for dementia. They noted that the optimal “dose” of walking to reduce the risk of dementia was just shy of 10,000 steps per day. Walking has also been tied to reduced risks of depression, [^53] diabetes, [^54] cardiovascular disease, [^55] and the incidence of some cancers, [^56] as well as increased survival after certain cancer diagnoses.

A paper published in Nature Medicine in 2022 found that walking 8,200 steps or more per day had a preventive effect against obesity, sleep apnea, gastroesophageal reflux disease, and major depressive disorder. [^57] That is a remarkable set of benefits for such a simple, zero-equipment, zero-cost activity. In other words: We should all be walking. A lot. If not every day, then almost every day.

A primary reason why walking is so beneficial is that it requires repeated muscular contractions. This activates an enzyme called AMPK. A 2018 paper by researchers at the Salk Institute for Biological Studies called AMPK the “guardian of metabolism,” and with good reason. [^58] This enzyme has multiple roles. It is involved in the process of stimulating glucose uptake into muscle cells. Animal research indicates that AMPK is also involved in generating more mitochondria through its interactions with PGC-1alpha, helps counter inflammation and improves vasodilation to help lower blood pressure and deliver more nutrients to cells, and under some conditions, can remove debris from them. [^59] Taking enough steps each day is therefore beneficial for health in numerous ways that extend way beyond just the calories burned by walking.

Data also support the value of interrupting long bouts of sitting with short bouts of walking. A large review from 2022 gathered data from seven studies that examined the health benefits of interrupting long bouts of sitting with either standing or walking. [^60] According to the analysis, standing between long stretches of sitting helps gradually lower glucose levels, but walking is far more effective.

Specifically, those researchers wanted to see which change is better at lowering glucose levels after meals. Walking is particularly effective right after a meal because glucose levels tend to increase at this time and preventing that rapid rise can help lower the risk of diabetes and heart disease. [^61] (High glucose levels are linked to both.) A review of eight randomized studies examining thirty different interventions in 116 people found that walking within thirty minutes after a meal lowers glucose levels more effectively than walking before a meal or after a break. [^62] That’s because we use glucose as energy… to walk. Moving therefore helps clear glucose out of the bloodstream, which is both protective to our vascular cells—our arteries, veins, and capillaries—and is beneficial for all the cells of our body by making them more effective energy utilizing machines, as described above. There is no need to rest right after eating. Just head straight out for that walk, even for just five minutes, although ten to twenty or even thirty minutes would be better.

We are talking about walking, not a workout. Just low-level, repeated muscle contractions. In fact, these contractions don’t even have to be created by walking: A 2022 study from the University of Houston found that repeated contractions of the soleus muscle, the deep muscle of our calf, significantly improve glucose regulation. [^63] Remarkably, this was found to be the case even if people remained seated and repeatedly raised their heel off the floor. It seems that even though the soleus is only about 1 percent of our total musculature, it has an outsized (positive) effect in regulating our glucose levels when it is repeatedly contracted by walking or “soleus pushups.” Of course, doing repeated soleus contractions while seated throughout the day, while possible, is not terribly compatible with daily life. Most people would not be able to concentrate on that while doing their work. But I include this recent finding here to emphasize just how powerful low-impact-repetitive muscle contractions can be. And of course, people who spend hours in meetings all day may want to consider doing calf raises while they’re confined to a desk. It’s not a replacement for walking, but it is certainly better than sitting still for long amounts of time.

What about standing still for long stretches of time? The study just described tells us that standing breaks are beneficial. Maybe you have a standing desk at your office, and that can be a great way to stretch your legs throughout the day. But walking is definitely better. A walk-and-work desk—where a treadmill fits underneath—can be a great way for some people to walk more. [^64]

Curiosity about the health benefits of walking has generated a tremendous amount of data. As mentioned above, we now have studies showing that walking reduces the risk of heart disease, hypertension, type 2 diabetes, cancer, cognitive impairment, death by pneumonia, poor sleep, mental health issues, stress, hormonal imbalances tied to aging, and more. [^65] Glucose regulation is certainly a part of it, but a deep dive into the molecular mechanisms behind all these effects is beyond the scope of this book. For those who are interested, a multidisciplinary team of researchers published a comprehensive review of the cellular mechanisms behind this wide range of effects.

There’s one more useful but nonobvious benefit to walking that I’d like to mention here. Walking induces optic flow, the state of having the visual image of the world slide past us. We are usually unaware of what this does to our nervous system. When we ambulate—nerd-speak for “walk”—a stream of visual input flows past us, an effect called global motion. [^66] Human and animal studies have found that forward ambulation causes reflexive lateral and repetitive (right-left-right…) eye movements that serve to stabilize the visual image on the eyes. Perhaps surprisingly, such eye movements significantly reduce neural activity in the amygdala, a region of our brain involved in threat detection. [^67] In fact repetitive lateralized eye movements are the cornerstone of trauma therapies such as EMDR (eye movement desensitization and reprocessing), which pairs left-right-left-right repetitive eye movements with the recounting of challenging experiences to uncouple their memory from the anxiety response. [^68] EMDR is done in a therapist’s office but was developed by psychologist Francine Shapiro, PhD, after she noticed that recounting traumatic experiences was made less stressful when the recounting took place on a walk. [^69] EMDR is still considered somewhat controversial in the therapy community. Some believe EMDR’s benefits come from the hypnosis-like state it can cause—and clinical hypnosis has well-established effects on mental health and brain rewiring. [^70] Others believe EMDR has its own direct effects on relief from trauma and depression. [^71] We need more data to parse all that. For now, however, it is interesting to note that walking makes the amygdala less active, thereby reducing stress and anxiety. [^72]

Alas, this benefit of walking won’t happen if you’re staring at your phone while doing it. That prevents the forward-ambulation-induced eye movements discussed here. The suppression of amygdala activity only occurs if we’re looking forward and around. I believe this phenomenon is one reason why spending time simply walking or hiking in nature is so tied to well-being. [^73] And also why walking or running on a treadmill—while better than not exercising—is less stress reducing than doing the same activity outdoors. The link between optic flow and stress reduction is an understudied area. However, walking outdoors is a zero-risk, zero-cost intervention that seems to translate to powerful results for your body and mental state.
In My Experience

I have a step tracker on both my phone and my WHOOP band (I’m an advisor for WHOOP). I track my steps every day but I don’t look at the data every day. I check it every few days to make sure I’m “hitting my numbers.” I know I get about seven thousand to ten thousand steps on average. More importantly, I am always seeking ways to take more steps. I make a point to pace indoors or walk outdoors whenever I take a phone call that doesn’t require me to be in front of my computer. I take stairs rather than escalators or elevators whenever I can. I see stairs as an opportunity, not a task, especially on travel days when I am going to be sitting a lot on the plane. I always strive to take two short walks of twenty to thirty minutes each during the day, usually one in the morning and one in the evening. If I miss the first one, I make the evening walk longer. I often take work calls, check in with friends or family, or listen to books or podcasts while I do. Every time we finish recording a podcast with a guest, our whole team takes a walk together (in the direction of the sun of course). If I have to sit a lot on a given day, I make it a point to walk a lot more the next day. I have an indoor treadmill for days when I can’t get outside to walk much due to work or weather.

I almost always use my standing desk to work at home. When I travel, I simply put my laptop on a box or stack of books on the desk or coffee table in the hotel room. It’s low-tech but it works, and I can rotate it toward the window to get more natural light. You need to find what works for you, of course.
COMMON QUESTIONS
How fast should I walk to get the health benefits of this activity

Any walking is better than no walking and brisk walking is better than slow walking. [^74] Taking all studies discussed above into account, walking briskly for at least thirty minutes per day and ideally forty to sixty minutes should be the goal. Walking at least five days a week and making an effort to take stairs, et cetera, appears to be sufficient activity to meet current recommended guidelines. [^75]

Again, walking is not “working out,” but it is the basis of any good exercise program. Think of it as necessary for your health. We were made to move. Getting steps each day is essential and should be part of your life. You can weave it into time in the yard, time with friends, time on the phone, and so on. And when you are stuck in a meeting or on a plane and can’t walk, try the calf raises discussed above. It’s discreet enough that you’re unlikely to get any strange looks.

Seven thousand steps are roughly an hour of walking, as I recommend, though obviously this will differ somewhat depending on the length of a person’s stride, the terrain, and walking speed. And, again, these steps do not need to be done all at once but rather can be spread throughout the day.
Aim to speed up as you incorporate walking more into your life. If you already walk often, then try to walk a little faster. Faster walking obtains health benefits in less time.
Are other types of low-impact movement, such as tai chi or slow swimming, as beneficial as walking

Yes and no. All movement is good movement, provided you don’t get injured. Doing ten air squats—going from standing to a seated position with your thighs parallel to the ground, then standing up again, and repeating that ten times—every forty-five minutes throughout the day for an 8.5-hour period has been shown to have even better glucose-lowering effects than thirty minutes of walking, which makes it a decent alternative when you can’t walk, like on really stormy days or on a long (or even a short) flight. [^76] The ten-air-squats-every-forty-five-minutes approach obviously does not provide all the benefits that walking outside does (like optic flow, fresh air, sunlight, etc.).

There are other types of low-impact, continuous physical activity to explore. Tai chi is great for balance and is often done near sunrise and outdoors, adding to the benefit for reasons discussed in both chapter 1 and chapter 5, and it’s typically done in groups, which has a positive social component. And tai chi certainly improves lower leg strength, balance, and coordination. [^77] That’s just one idea, but of course there are many others.
Everyone needs to find a low-impact, continuous physical activity that works for them in terms of enjoyment, and compatibility with lifestyle.

That being said, I’ll come back to walking. Walking is a movement that draws on many different aspects of our anatomy: It puts weight on our skeletal structure, which is good for helping maintain our bone density and strength; it engages the soleus, which as mentioned before has a positive effect on glucose regulation; and it has the added bonus of optic flow for mental health. Add walking into your life wherever and whenever possible. Again, don’t think of it as exercise, think of it as nonnegotiable movement that is foundational to a healthy day. Does that mean walking is the only thing we need to do? Of course not. In the context of physical activity, and to use scientific jargon, it is “necessary but not sufficient” for your health. So let’s now discuss the things to do in addition to walking, starting with three times per week resistance training. Done properly.
EXERCISE PROTOCOL 2 Resistance Train Three Times per Week
WHAT TO DO
• Adhere to a program, starting with this foundational template that features three resistance training sessions every seven days.
• Day 1: Cardiovascular training (explained in Exercise Protocol 3)

• Day 2: Resistance training of major lower body muscles: quadriceps, hamstrings, calves Your glutes, core, and lower back are indirectly trained this day given the nature of the exercises involved, but direct glute training can be added.
• Day 3: Rest day
• Day 4: Resistance training of major torso muscles: chest, back, abdominals, and core (optional neck)
• Day 5: Cardiovascular training (explained in Exercise Protocol 3)
• Day 6: Cardiovascular training (explained in Exercise Protocol 3)
• Day 7: Resistance training of shoulders, biceps, triceps, abdominals/core (optional forearms and neck)
HOW IT WORKS

This template is, in my experience, the best place to start and in many cases stay to achieve all-around fitness: strength, endurance, speed, and power. And it can be tailored to deliver the aesthetic changes you want. It is grounded in the fundamental principles of effective resistance training, [^78] and I strongly believe it offers the best time-and-effort to results ratio. It can also be easily modified when your schedule gets busy or you need a week off. I have seen it work for everyone I’ve suggested it to.

This program consists of three sessions of resistance training every seven days. It also includes three cardiovascular training sessions, done on non–resistance training days. (These are detailed in the next protocol. I include them in the template overview for clarity.) Together, these sessions provide the right amount of directed stress and recovery.

If you are already familiar with resistance training, you may think you need more sets to gain muscle or more training days for certain target areas than what this protocol suggests. Keep in mind that each session works in the larger context of the program. They synergize. For example, you’ll train your legs but four days later, you’ll sprint or row or cycle at an intensity that also taxes your legs (just enough, not too much). You won’t lose ground.

For those new to resistance training, I highly suggest you do the “break-in” period, like the one detailed in Mike Mentzer’s point number four in the introduction to this chapter. This will help you develop proper form with the exercises you select. For those experienced with resistance training, or novices who have completed the “break-in” period, you should design the specifics of each resistance training session with these variables as guidelines:
WORKOUT DURATION: ABOUT 60 +/– 20 MINUTES
• Brief whole-body warm-up: About 5 minutes
• Total number of warm-up sets: 1–3 per exercise
• Total number of work sets per muscle group: 4–9
• Total number of exercises per muscle group: 2–3
• For each major muscle group: Do at least one exercise that is a compound (multi-joint) exercise and one that is an isolation (one-joint) exercise. A third compound movement can be added, if needed.
• Total number of work sets per exercise: 2–3 sets (usually just 2)

• Repetition (“reps”) range per set: As a general guideline, aim to use enough resistance so you reach “failure” after doing 6–10 reps of a given compound exercise, or in the case of an isolation exercise, after 8–15 reps. But if you can only get 5 reps, do that. Or if you can continue past 10 or 15 reps (reps in good form, that is!), keep going until you reach failure. Don’t stop simply because you’ve reached a given number of reps. Remember, too, that you must use progressive overload to get results. Once you can perform 10 reps of a compound exercise, or 10–15 of an isolation exercise, in perfect form, you’ll want to increase the amount of weight for work sets of that exercise in the next workout, which will very likely reduce the number of reps you can do until you progress further, and so on. This is absolutely key!

Note: The rep ranges discussed here and throughout this protocol are just guidelines; venturing into heavier 3–5 reps or lighter 15–25 repetition ranges makes good sense for some exercises. So does systematically varying between very specific rep ranges for four to eight weeks at a time.
• Rest duration between warm-up sets: 1–2 minutes

• Rest duration between work sets: 2–5 minutes, depending on repetition range. Typically people rest longer (3–5 minutes) between work sets of compound exercises than between work sets of isolation exercises (90 seconds–3 minutes), and I suggest you do the same.

On reading the above list I imagine novices might already be confused and experienced resistance trainers already might be furrowing their brows, but let’s consider each of these points so the rationale is clear.
WORKOUT DURATION: ABOUT 60 +/– 20 MINUTES

You’re in the gym to resistance train, and you’re resistance training to trigger specific neural, muscular, and connective tissue adaptations. For most people the specific adaptations they seek are increased strength and perhaps also hypertrophy, or increased muscle size. Many want to also lose body fat.

It may surprise you to learn that body fat loss isn’t a specific adaptation from doing a certain type of training. Why not? Because body fat loss is mostly the consequence of being in a caloric deficit. In chapter 4, I explain how certain foods and food combinations often make us want to eat more or less, but it’s caloric intake that determines if we maintain, lose, or gain weight.

Some people say they want to get toned, and others say they want to get jacked, or ripped. For the record: Toned is not an actual exercise adaptation either, but instead refers to a defined-yet-still-slender aesthetic. And while we’re talking nonscientific but commonly heard fitness terms: Jacked means larger, rounded muscles and relatively lean, and ripped means still muscular and extra lean. Leanness comes from a combination of training and nutrition, but mostly nutrition. The program here is great for gaining muscle, maintaining muscle while losing body fat, or for gaining muscle and losing body fat, depending on how you adjust your caloric intake.

Many people of course also resistance train for the general adaptation benefits discussed earlier in this chapter, including improved brain and body health and longevity, elevated mood, better sleep, and so on.

Unless you’re socializing or texting or taking endless selfies, or the gym is packed, your resistance training sessions should rarely last longer than about 60 +/– 20 minutes. After a five-minute whole-body warm-up, and then two to three warm-up sets for your first exercise, sixty to eighty minutes of effortful, highly focused “work sets” is more than enough to stimulate the specific and general adaptations you’re seeking. And that includes the rest periods between work sets too.

Why not longer? Because after eighty minutes of hard resistance training, the fatigue and stress on your body and nervous system is typically greater than is conducive for recovery before your next workout. Also, after eighty minutes, it can be hard to generate the focus and effort needed to continue to stimulate specific adaptations safely. While you might have the energy to train longer, it’s good to finish your workout with some vigor left to devote to other aspects of life. Most people will find they won’t progress much faster by training for longer sessions, or even more frequent sessions (and in many cases, they stop getting results altogether or even start regressing!). Especially when trying to incorporate the necessary cardiovascular training session discussed in Exercise Protocol 3. By resistance training three times a week for an hour or so, you’re far more likely to be consistent over the long-term, which is ultimately what matters to both results now and in the future. There are times when because of long rest periods needed between sets in a crowded gym, workouts can take ninety minutes. Don’t fret about it, but don’t make that the norm. In fact, if you can get a great workout done in fewer than sixty minutes, even better.
Here are a few more nonobvious things that make a big difference to increase your efficiency in the gym:
A note about “intensity” and soreness

People sometimes think that being really sore in the days after a workout is the goal, but it’s not. Delayed onset muscle soreness is not a requirement to make progress. Your goal is to effectively stress your muscles and nervous system across the training session, while still being able to recover before your next training session. This is how you continue to progressively overload your muscles each time you resistance train… and that’s how you make progress.

Remember, done right, resistance training is a very potent stressor. Usually stress has a negative connotation, but in the context of exercise, just the right amount of local and systemic stress is what will bring you results quickly and consistently. That’s why I designed this template with plenty of time for your muscles and connective tissues, and also your nervous system, to recover. Your goal is to trigger the proper adaptations by training really hard, then get out of the gym and recover while you live your life.
Don’t think “workout,” think “training”

First, training is, as the definition of the word implies, practicing. As Pavel Tsatsouline, world-renowned strength coach, explained on my podcast, it’s best to view and engage in resistance training as if it were a self-taught class wherein you practice the skill of triggering specific adaptations. [^79] The huge advantage of this approach is that it keeps you from adopting the “working out” mindset, which has most people merely going through the motions, thinking about burning more calories or the pump, or just getting through the workout. That mindset confuses effort with directed effort. And this template is all about directed effort designed to trigger specific adaptations. Calling it training carries a different level of seriousness that, in my experience, translates to higher quality effort and results. If someone asks “Training for what?” you can tell them, “to get stronger” or simply “life!”
Track your progress

Treating your resistance training as a self-taught class means you should track your progress. This helps you remember what you did last session so that you can make sure you’re properly using progressive overload. I believe that whether you are a novice or highly experienced, you should take your training seriously—it’s your body and your health after all.

Some people will track their sets and reps and the amount of weight they use on each exercise on their phone, others in a training notebook, others using an app. It doesn’t really matter, although the phone offers so many chances for distraction whereas a good ol’ pen and some paper have far fewer.

I usually put my phone on airplane mode when I start my workouts and only use it for music, or I simply train without it. Some people like to listen to a podcast or book while they train. You decide what is best for you but, again, take your training seriously. Avoid texting and scrolling social media while you’re training.
