Your workouts will likely be much more effective, and I can guarantee you they will be more efficient. I use a paper notebook to write down every set and number of reps I do in order to track my progress, as described above. This makes a tremendous difference because it gives you a specific goal to beat every exercise and set. It also makes it fun. You can strive for and see objective progress in almost every workout.

Many people are haphazard about their training. Thus, they get some results when they start, but their progress quickly evaporates. It takes the same amount of time (or even potentially less) to do a truly effective workout as it does to do a half-baked one. So make sure you do the former. The great news is that as you practice resistance training, you get better at it.
BRIEF WHOLE-BODY WARM-UP: ABOUT 5 MINUTES

You’ll get better results and avoid injury by including a brief five-minute whole-body warm-up at the start of each resistance training session. The goal is simply to increase your core body temperature a few degrees, to loosen up (a nontechnical term) your joints and to prepare for the sets to follow. I like to pedal on a stationary bike or walk briskly on a treadmill for five minutes until I break a light sweat. Alternatively, you can do jumping jacks, windmills, or get on the elliptical or stair climber. It doesn’t really matter as long as you warm up. Physical therapist Kelly Starrett, PhD—famous for his work on mobility and all-around fitness—offered a great warm-up when he was a guest on my podcast, especially for when you’re feeling less-than-motivated to train:

Just play for a few minutes. Shoot some layups and free throws on a basketball court, or shadow box, skip rope, or complete a simple circuit of body-weight-only exercises: first twenty-five air squats, followed by five lunges per side with just your body weight, and then jog in place for a minute before repeating, until five minutes have elapsed. [^80]

You may recall that bodily movement activates two circuits: one in the body and the other in the brain. These trigger the release of adrenaline and norepinephrine, respectively, which in turn makes you more physically energized and mentally alert. [^81] That’s the other reason to do a brief whole-body warm-up. Many people find they are dragging themselves to the gym, and, after warming up, they feel like a new person. Some of that is psychological, but there is a physiological component too—the way that whole body movement stimulates adrenaline (via the body-to-brain connection) “wakes up” your brain, as we discussed at the start of this chapter. [^82]
TOTAL NUMBER OF WARM-UP SETS: 1–3 SETS
Warm-up sets ensure that you are performing an exercise correctly across a full range of motion, and they prepare your nervous system, muscles, and connective tissues for the work sets that follow.

Most people do relatively high reps for their warm-up sets: For instance, they will do fifteen to twenty reps on the first warm-up set, add some resistance and do ten to fifteen reps more, then add a bit more resistance and do six to ten reps for the last warm-up set. Most people also tend to rest briefly between their warm-up sets, usually no more than thirty seconds.

I suggest doing warm-up sets differently, so you can get more out of your work sets that follow. Regardless of the repetition range you have planned for your subsequent work sets, make your first warm-up set only six to ten reps. Use a moderately light weight for you, around 40 percent of the amount of resistance you will use for your first work set. Lift and lower the weight under control throughout every set to make sure that you mentally engage the muscles you are trying to train. Then rest one to two minutes, and do a second warm-up set, but this time perform only four to eight reps using about 65 percent of the weight you’ll use for your first work set. For some people that’s enough warm-up before the first work set. If your work sets are going to be heavy on a given exercise, meaning they will have you reaching failure (that is, again, the inability to continue moving the weight in good form) after completing just five to seven reps, then I suggest you rest an additional one to two minutes after your second warm-up set and do a third and final warm-up set. For that third warm-up, use about 75 percent of the weight you’ll use on your first work set. And for that third warm-up set, keep the reps low, to only two to four. Yes, you could do more, but that’s not the goal. You’re not trying to stimulate any adaptations with your warm-up sets. Rather, think of them—and especially that third warm-up set—as rehearsals for the real deal: the work sets to follow. Warm-up sets are about preparing your body and mind for the work sets.

Note the percentages above are approximate percentages of the weight you plan to use for your first work set, not a percentage of your one-repetition maximum (1RM), or the maximum you can lift once in good form. Most importantly, your warm-up set should never come close to failure.
TOTAL NUMBER OF WORK SETS PER MUSCLE GROUP: 4–9 SETS

To be clear: When I say muscle group I’m referring, for example, to your shoulders, or biceps, or hamstrings, or triceps, or quadriceps. “Arms” are not a muscle group. Nor are “legs.” At least not in the context of resistance-training jargon. Quadriceps are called a “muscle group” because they are made up of several muscles. The same applies to your biceps and all the rest. Later in the chapter I provide links to exercise videos that will clarify any confusion about this and what exercises to select when training. Doing four to nine work sets per muscle group (divided across two to three different exercises) is more than enough to effectively trigger the specific adaptations you want, if you focus and work hard to control the resistance throughout every rep of every work set until you can’t move the weight any more, aka failure.
So should you do four or eight, or five, or seven sets?

You decide, but be logical about it based on your goals and needs. One thing that is rarely discussed but important in designing the best program for you is that many people have muscle groups that, for a variety of reasons related to their genetics, the sports they played as youth, or their resistance training history, respond much faster to resistance training than other muscle groups. It makes sense to do fewer total work sets for those muscle groups. You heard me. Do fewer work sets for your quicker-to-respond muscle groups. That will ensure you don’t throw off your proportions and create strength imbalances that eventually will lead to injuries. Women seem to be much better about training for aesthetic balance than men. We have all seen “that guy”—the one with the big chest and arms but disproportionately much smaller legs, or the one whose shoulders and back are as wide as barn doors, but with a tiny neck that makes it look like his head is on the wrong body. It’s not just about aesthetics; muscle strength and size imbalances set you up for injuries in and out of the gym.

Aim for strength and aesthetic balance. If you have a muscle group that responds easily, limit yourself to doing four to five or even just three work sets total for that muscle group in a given workout. You should still focus on training to failure and in great form during those sets. For all other muscle groups, I suggest you do four to eight total work sets.

One last point regarding the total number of work sets to do. The better you focus and contract a given muscle group, the fewer work sets it will take to stimulate the specific adaptations you’re after. Think about it this way: If you’ve ever hammered a nail into wood, you know that one to two clean, well-placed strikes of the hammer drives the nail in flush. If you don’t hit the nail squarely on the head, however, you need many more swings. When you do four to eight work sets per muscle group, and just two to three work sets per exercise, focusing from start to finish as you lift and lower the resistance, your task of triggering specific adaptations in that muscle group is complete. Additional sets are not needed and might do more damage than good—just as continuing to pound on a nail that is already hammered in simply damages the wood.

How do you measure your neuromuscular control? Jeff Cavaliere, a physical therapist and strength and conditioning coach who worked with the New York Mets before founding his own online exercise platform, AthleanX, has a cool trick that translates to more effective (adaptation-stimulating) workouts too. Can you contract a muscle, let’s say your bicep or calf or quadricep hard enough to make it almost feel like a cramp but with no added resistance, just by “flexing” the target muscle? If so, that is good news because when you train using isolation exercises, that’s effectively what you are trying to do. You’re just adding resistance to contract the muscle even harder, throughout the entire movement. This one takes some time for people to wrap their heads around because everyone thinks about “lifting weights,” but effective resistance training aimed at generating hypertrophy and strength improvements is about challenging muscles, and the weight or resistance is just a tool to allow you to do that more effectively.

Compound exercises challenge specific groups of muscles and also train the coordinated action of those muscles as they work together to perform certain movements. A squat, for instance, calls on the muscles of the quadriceps, hamstrings (somewhat), glutes and lower back, and numerous stabilizer muscles. “Feeling” your quadriceps during a squat is crucial but the expectation is not that you completely isolate them; in fact, that’s impossible. That is why in this program I suggest doing both compound and isolation exercises.

And if you can’t feel the muscle you’re trying to target when doing compound exercises, consider doing the isolation exercise for that muscle group first, then the compound exercise for that muscle group. For example, if you are having a hard time feeling your chest (pectoralis) muscles during your bench presses, do some sort of chest-isolation exercise first, then move to your bench presses. You don’t have to move immediately from one to the other in classic “pre-exhaustion” format. You can simply do your one to three work sets of a chest-isolation movement and then do your one to three work sets of bench presses or other compound movement for the chest.

By the way, if you’re feeling lost with these mentions of exercise names or anything else, do not worry! I provide numerous examples of isolation and compound exercises at protocolsbook.com/videos. You’ll of course have to use less weight on the compound movement if you do an isolation movement for the same muscle group first, but remember why you are there in the first place: to trigger specific adaptations in specific muscle groups. And you can always reverse the order and proceed with the compound movement a few months later, once you have established a strong mind-muscle-connection with that formerly hard-to-feel and hard-to-improve muscle group.

Is it possible to do too few sets? Yes. [^83] Or I should say, most trainers would say yes. Arthur Jones and Mike Mentzer were famous for taking the low-volume–high-intensity logic to the extreme, arguing that people should do just one to two work sets per muscle group per week. That was their suggestion: not per exercise but across the entire workout! Most everyone agrees nowadays (and the science does too) that you need more work sets. Studies over the last two decades reinforce the idea that somewhere more in the range of four to eight work sets per muscle group is both necessary and sufficient to trigger near maximal strength and/or hypertrophy adaptations. [^84]

Many people try to train each muscle group twice per week, with twelve to twenty work sets per group at each session, believing that this is the “optimal” frequency for stimulating muscle growth. But believe me: Doing fewer sets with more intensity, with the focus described here, three times per week, allows for a more sustainable practice and thus better results over time. I will die on this hill! And again, the goal is to do cardiovascular workouts three times a week, too, some of which are intense. That mix is essential for health and is covered in Exercise Protocol 3.
And the great part about this program is that you still end up targeting each muscle group twice per week, just not the way you might think. Let me explain.

As I mentioned above, with regard to frequency of training, you can find studies that argue training each muscle group two or even three times per week is best for these results. [^85] I suggest resistance training for each major muscle group directly only once per week. This is not by accident. By scheduling this way along with specific types of cardiovascular training sessions on particular days, you actually end up training each muscle group twice per week: once directly, and once indirectly. On chest and back day, your shoulders and arms get some indirect training. On shoulders and arms day, your chest and back get some indirect training too—because you are doing compound movements like overhead presses and dips and perhaps also some palms-facing-you pull-ups for your biceps. On “sprint” cardio day (covered in Protocol 3), your legs get indirect stimulation, and if you do your sprints on an assault bike, those stationary bikes with a fan and handles that you pump forward and back while you pedal, your back and arms get some additional indirect training too. Of course, these indirect training sessions are not enough to stimulate maximal strength or hypertrophy increases on their own, but they synergize beautifully with the direct resistance training that you’re already doing for a total of three days a week with weights. A sprint four days after a proper leg workout for calves, quadriceps, hamstrings, and glutes, with multiple sets taken to failure… you’ll be able to do that, I promise, but it’s right as your legs start to feel fresh again… and a few days later you’re back to your leg workout. You won’t lose ground. In fact, you’ll come out ahead on both. Try it.

In my experience, the overall program in this chapter provides a well-rounded combination of strength, hypertrophy, endurance, and flexibility and is the best time investment to achieve the results most people are seeking. It also keeps your motivation level for each workout high, which is crucial for anyone leading a busy life. Going to the gym for hard workouts five days a week is difficult for most to maintain. Pretty soon, people are downing two energy drinks and a coffee just to get going, not sleeping well, and getting sick. But three days a week, with just two to three hard work sets per exercise and two to three exercises per muscle group and three or four muscle groups? That’s something I’m confident you can do for the rest of your life—and that’s how to think of both getting and staying in great shape. It’s for all these reasons that I strongly believe in this program. Let me put it this way: I’ve given this program to men and women of a wide range of ages, athletic backgrounds, and health histories, and I’ve never seen it not work for them to reach their fitness (and aesthetic) goals.
TOTAL NUMBER OF EXERCISES PER MUSCLE GROUP: 2–3 EXERCISES TOTAL NUMBER OF WORK SETS PER EXERCISE: 2–3 SETS (USUALLY JUST 2)

In most cases, doing two exercises that target each muscle group is plenty, but in some cases you may want to do a third exercise if it’s a muscle group of particular focus. Once again and so that we’re clear on terms: Legs are not one muscle group. Quadriceps are. Hamstrings are another muscle group. Your legs have quadriceps, hamstrings, glutes, and calves—each of which has its own subdivisions. You do two to three exercises for each of these groups.

It’s crucial that at least one of the two to three exercises for a muscle group be a compound (multi-joint) exercise. In most cases you’ll also want to do one isolation (single joint) exercise for the same muscle group. Doing two to three exercises (with two to three work sets for each exercise) brings you to four to nine work sets per muscle group. (I recommend not going above nine work sets total for a single muscle group in a workout, given that you are training multiple muscle groups in each workout. Indeed, aiming for six hard work sets per muscle group per workout is often better, provided that at least three of those sets are from a compound exercise and you take those work sets to failure.)

Time constraints will often dictate exactly how much you do. So will how well you slept (I suggest aiming for the lower end of the number of sets on days when you are a bit sleep-deprived, but still doing the compound movements). So will nutrition. And stress. If you’re well rested, fed, and you have the time, do the full three exercises for two to three work sets each, for six to nine total work sets. Or just do four to six work sets per muscle group total and pour every bit of focus and energy into those. With time, you’ll learn when enough is enough for that muscle group on a given day and according to the context of the rest of your life.
Specific exercise selection

As mentioned earlier, target a muscle group with at least one compound exercise and one isolation exercise for that same muscle group. (I provide a set of video tutorials and options to select from at protocolsbook.com/videos).

The rationale for including one of each is that compound exercises target a given muscle in conjunction with other muscles that it normally works with in various everyday movements. That also means compound movements allow you to use heavier weights, which provide not just a direct effect on the muscles you’re training but also a positive “systemic effect” on various hormones and neurotransmitter systems of the brain and body. [^86] And because they mimic a lot of pushing, pulling, kneeling, and lunging movements we do in everyday life, compound movements carry over to “real world” strength. The ones done standing, like squats and dead lifts, overhead presses, and even bicep curls or overhead extensions, help in developing more core stability and strength too. Taken to failure for two to three well-controlled, focused sets per muscle group, compound exercises are great… but they are pretty taxing on your nervous system. This is especially important considering you are doing at least one such movement, and perhaps even two, per muscle group, and training multiple muscle groups per workout.

Follow with an isolation exercise for each major muscle group. It lets you intensely target a specific muscle, it reinforces the mind-muscle connection to that muscle, and, because of the mechanics of the movement (the position and range of motion, etc.), isolation exercises tend to develop aspects of the target muscle that compound movements may not target as thoroughly.

And they don’t create quite as much overall stress on your nervous system. Yes, exercise-induced stress is good (!) but it adds up and, as stated earlier, you have just one nervous system for both your workouts and for the other aspects of your life. You don’t want to overtax it. That does not mean go easy on isolation exercises. You still need to use progressive overload and to take those isolation exercise sets to failure. By the way, once you do two work sets of leg extensions or side lateral raises (an isolation movement for the shoulders) for twelve to fifteen well-controlled reps to true failure, you’ll realize that isolation movements done properly are their own special kind of intense!

To illustrate the importance of exercise and complementarity, let’s return to that earlier example and talk about training your quadriceps. You’re choosing two exercises. The compound exercise could be a barbell back (or front) squat (your hip and knee joints both move in a squat; hence, multi-joint), and the isolation exercise could be the leg extension machine (only your knee joint moves and your hips stay locked). If you have the energy that day, you might also do another two to three work sets of a compound exercise for your quadriceps, such as leg presses or hack squats.

As you likely realize by now, the exercises you can select from are nearly endless. And they can be free weight or you can use weight machines, or even just your body weight for some of them, like pull-ups or barbell dips. What’s important is that you can do a movement safely, without pain, and while still pushing yourself to failure. And that you can safely add more and more resistance to the movement over time as you get stronger. People debate exercise selection a lot. Assuming you include both compound and isolation movements, you have to find what is best for you. What equipment you have access to is of course also a factor. Again, the video links I provide give you lots of options. In the meantime, let’s discuss the “best exercise” myth.
The “best exercise/movement” myth

Barbell squats (where the bar is on your shoulders as you squat down and stand up again) are a terrific compound exercise many people can and should use to target their quadriceps, glutes, and other leg muscles. They challenge your lower back and core muscles too. Some trainers will say that you absolutely must do them, but that’s simply not true. Some people have hip, leg, or shoulder mechanics that prevent them from doing barbell back squats without joint pain during the exercise or in the days after. You could work with a trainer to overcome those issues, but you could also substitute front squats, where the bar is held on the front of your shoulders, or hack machine squats, which have your back on an angled sled for support, or even leg presses for your quadriceps instead. There are Zercher squats, rear-leg-elevated squats, and goblet squats. There are also a near-endless number of lunge variations that target the quadriceps, glutes, and other muscles emphasized in the barbell back squat. The internet is filled with exercise clips showing all of these exercises. Again, I provide video tutorials of many to choose from at protocolsbook.com/videos.

Find the exercises you can really push yourself in, without joint pain. You’ll enjoy it more, and your results will be greater… which will lead you to enjoy it even more. You’ll experience a whole different relationship to resistance training if you make yourself the CEO of the process. Only do exercises that really work for your body. Just don’t only do isolation movements. Compound movements are necessary to get the full benefits of resistance training.
A few quick notes about safety and pain

Safety: I’ll be direct about this. Be careful as you train. Done correctly (warm up, don’t add more weight than you can handle with control, and so on) and with caution to avoid a few potentially perilous mistakes, resistance training as described in this protocol is a very safe activity.

What sort of perilous mistakes am I referring to? Well, people have died barbell bench-pressing. [^87] They couldn’t push the bar up from their chest and they asphyxiated. It’s rare, but it happens. Have a spotter who knows how to spot you correctly—which means they have to be strong enough to pull the loaded bar up off your chest or neck if need be. If you don’t have someone who can do that, an easy solution is to use dumbbells if you’re bench-pressing alone—those can be set down to your knees and dropped to your sides if you hit failure. A few dents in the floor are far better than the alternative. Or use a rack with safety pins (sturdy bars that can support a loaded bar) to set the weight on if you hit failure mid-repetition. Same goes for barbell squats. Yes, you can “dump” the bar behind you if you hit failure, but far better to have a knowledgeable spotter. If no such person is around, again use a rack with pins so you can set the bar down and crawl out. Many people opt for machines like the leg press or hack squat for compound quadriceps movements for just this reason: It’s easier to hit failure without doing what I described. And they usually have “stops” you can engage when you hit failure. No, these movements do not engage the same muscles to the same degree as free weight compound exercises. Yes, they are safer. You decide your risk tolerance, but be safe regardless.

Also, think about your posture every time you are picking up or putting down weights, even if you’re just replacing them on the rack or getting in position to start your set. A lot of resistance training injuries are the consequence of people not being mindful as they do the in-between work sets stuff because their mind is someplace else.

I’m proud of the fact that I have been training hard, and heavy (for me) for nearly thirty-five years and have never had a serious injury from resistance training. (Knock on wood!) Sure, I’ve had a few minor strains here and there but nothing that floored me or kept me from training or daily activities for more than a few days. I attribute that to staying mentally focused from start to finish in the gym, and to only making relatively small incremental increases (5 to 10 percent) in the amount of weight I add to any given movement from week to week, and only once I can do at least eight to twelve reps of that movement in good form.

Pain: We have all heard the mantra “no pain, no gain.” News flash (!): That does not refer to joint or connective tissue pain. It refers to the burning sensation in muscles caused primarily by the accumulation of hydrogen ions inside muscle cells, brought on by the fact that the muscle cells need energy faster than oxygen can be delivered to them. (No, not lactic acid as was once believed. Lactate is created, but we know now it is not the cause of the burning.) [^88] If an exercise causes sharp or dull joint pain—not post exercise soreness but, again, pain—either your form or the exercise itself is not right. Don’t persist with that exercise. At least not that day. Find an alternative.
REPETITION (“REPS”) RANGE PER SET

When it comes to selecting the number of reps to do for your work sets, you have options. After decades of debate about “optimal rep ranges,” research from Brad Schoenfeld’s lab, at Lehman College, found that using repetition ranges of anywhere from five all the way up to thirty on work sets stimulates essentially the same amount of hypertrophy. That is, if (and only if!) those sets are taken to failure. [^89] Generally speaking, this is great news because it means that if you select a weight that you think you’ll do eight reps with (and fail on rep nine) but somehow you are able to do eleven reps (and fail on rep twelve), you’ll still make progress. It removes the need to stay in a narrow rep range, at least for hypertrophy.

At face value, these findings suggest you don’t ever need to train with low reps and heavy weights to get results; you simply need to push until the final reps of your work set are very hard to complete. In some sense, yes, you can use moderate or even light weights (for you) that limit you to twelve to thirty reps before reaching failure. But you should also regularly use heavy (for you) weights, which means weights that limit you to just five to eight reps and no more, despite your maximum effort to complete more. Turns out using a mix of weights stimulates different muscle fiber types and ensures you activate different forms of cellular stress and thus adaptations. [^90]
More on that below but in the meantime, if you don’t want to have to think much about rep range selection, here’s a good guide:
For compound exercises, use the amount of weight on your work sets that has you reaching failure between five and twelve reps.
• Occasionally use heavier loads that limit you to just 3–5 reps before you reach failure.

• Experiment with lighter loads that allow you to complete higher repetition compound exercises, especially for quadriceps and calves. Many people find that 12–20 repetition squats (or its variations) are very effective for hypertrophy.

• Warning: High-repetition quadriceps work sets taken to failure are brutal. The loads you use will be lighter than you would use for 5–10 reps taken to failure, but the pain tolerance level on the final reps (and mental fortitude) required for 15–25 reps of a compound leg movement, like squats or even one of its machine variations, like a hack squat, taken to failure is no joke.
For isolation exercises, use an amount of weight on your work sets that has you reaching failure between eight and fifteen reps.

• Doing isolation exercises for heavier 5-8 repetition sets (to failure) is not bad per se, but most people find that doing higher (8–15, or as many as 25) reps on isolation movements like leg extensions, shoulder lateral raises, preacher curls for biceps, and so on, is more effective. But feel free to experiment. You may find, for instance, that your hamstrings respond best to heavier sets of lying leg curls (an isolation exercise) that limit you to 5-7 reps.
Just remember, no matter what the repetition range you use for a movement, go to failure on work sets, even if it has you exceeding your target repetition range for that day and exercise.

Now before you say, “I heard leaving one to three ‘reps in reserve’ (RIR) is just as good as training to failure,” we need to get honest: If you use heavy (for you) weights that would make you reach failure somewhere between five and ten reps, but you stop a rep or two before failure, you probably will still stimulate some strength and hypertrophy adaptations. That is because heavier loads generate levels of mechanical tension that readily stimulate muscle and nerve-to-muscle adaptations. [^91] However, given that this program has you doing relatively fewer work sets (four to nine), and directly targeting each major muscle group only once per week (and a second time per week, indirectly, as described above), you really should take all your work sets to failure.

Still not convinced? Well, consider this reality: We all like to think we are training our absolute hardest, but what most people consider taking a set to failure almost always leaves one to two more repetitions in reserve. How can I be so sure? Well, if you hit failure on the eighth rep of a set but were told that getting a ninth rep would save someone’s life, I am willing to bet that ninth rep would happen. So failure is somewhat subjective. Thankfully lives are not on the line according to when we reach failure on our lifts. But that momentary muscular failure is the closest thing you have to an objective measure of intensity of effort. So seek it out.

Here’s a bit more information so you can make the best-informed decisions about whether to train heavy, moderate, or light (for you). Hypertrophy adaptations are thought to be stimulated by at least three things: [^92]

• 1 Microdamage caused to the muscles using heavier loads. (Here, we can define “heavier loads” as sets that have you fail after completing three to six reps.) The extent to which this contributes to hypertrophy is a matter of emerging debate, but it still has some solid evidence in its favor.
• 2 Mechanical tension (from moderate to heavy loads and/or the contraction or stretching of the target muscle).

• 3 Metabolic stress (including the pump and cellular swelling, all brought on by enhanced blood flow, along with the release and delivery of various cellular factors to the muscles you are training).

Muscle size and strength are correlated so if you make a muscle bigger it will get stronger, but training specifically to maximize strength is typically done by using loads that limit you to three to five reps (or fewer) and doing a large number of sets for each muscle across the week and not training to failure on any one set. Getting strong is great but the vast majority of people who resistance train do so to get stronger and for aesthetic changes that are best brought about by the rep and load ranges discussed above.

That is why I suggest you mainly use five to twelve reps on your compound work sets, and occasionally venture into using heavier loads that limit you to just three to five reps before you fail. In reality there will be times when you can do ten reps of a movement with a given weight, so you increase the amount of weight the next time you’re training that body part and somehow you can only do three or four reps before you reach failure. Don’t worry about it. Just keep striving to add more reps or weight each workout in great form. If you want to obsess over something useful, obsess over the amount of focused effort you put into your work sets and using great form!

About ten years ago, I decided to train exclusively with heavy weights that limited me to three to five reps on compound exercises and six to ten reps on isolation exercises—which is called periodization. I did that for three months and I got a lot stronger, such that when I went back to doing five to twelve reps, I was stronger on every movement. Later I ran a similar experiment using lighter weights and more reps (12–25) for a few months… all still to failure on work sets of course. I made considerable progress in terms of hypertrophy, but when I went back to using heavier weights for lower reps, I found I had lost a lot of ground. So I learned something. Nowadays I almost always train with weights that limit me to five to twelve reps and only venture up to fifteen to twenty for an especially intense leg workout or on certain upper body isolation exercises. That’s what is best for me and my goals. You should experiment and find what is best for you.
Progressive overload is key!

I know that the requirement for progressive overload is a giant “duh” to many of you out there, but others may need this reminder. If you do the same workout every week, using the same weights, reps, and sets, take note. You might sweat, work hard, and feel the mood enhancements of exercise but your progress will halt. Because we’re keeping the work sets to just two or three, you must challenge your muscles by either increasing the amount of weight or the number of reps, or both, while keeping your form excellent.
“More weight or more reps, perfect form, and pushing to failure.” That should be your resistance training mantra!

Be aware that it’s unreasonable to expect to add weight while maintaining the same rep count you performed the previous week, but it will happen. Those are great workouts. However, there will be weeks when, for whatever reason, you are not able to hit your target weight and rep goals in the gym. Consider the reasons: Are you sleep-deprived? Underfed, under caffeinated? Unfocused? Life happens, so don’t obsess about it. Just do your absolute best for that day. If you find you’re not making progress for two weeks in a row, you may need to reduce the set volume. Yes, I said it: Try doing fewer work sets and see if that budges you forward. Or maybe it’s time for a week off to rest, so you can come back stronger.

Finally, while 1RM lifts and even 2RM lifts are great for building strength (and allow you to answer the “How much can you bench?” question you’ll invariably get at some point), I recommend most people avoid doing 1RMs. They come with too much risk of injury. If you really want to do them, fine, but use a spotter, please! And understand that 1RM lifts are what you train for in powerlifting—which is a specific sport. If that’s what you’re interested in, there are great programs out there for powerlifting. But most people are lifting weights for other reasons. They want the variety of benefits that come from the resistance training I’ve described here. If someone ever asks me how much I can bench, I usually just tell them what I did for five to eight reps the preceding week because that’s all I know for certain!
An important note about training to, and past, failure

As I’ve said about a hundred times now (but still a hundred fewer than Mentzer would have in the same time frame!): Do the first work set of an exercise to failure, using perfect form. Pour everything you have into that set, on every repetition. That means, as the final reps approach, think: “This is what stimulates the adaptations I’m here for.” Strive to keep your form stricter, and stress the targeted muscles more, not less as failure approaches. Then, when the weight won’t move any more, try HARD to continue to move it for an additional three to five seconds, then re-rack the weight.

Then rest two to three minutes, or perhaps even four to five minutes on compound exercises for legs or back or other large muscles. Then do a second set of that exercise, also to failure, but don’t fight to push the weight once you’ve hit failure, like I described for the first work set above. This is not a back-off set. You’re just stopping when you can’t move the weight anymore.

Should you do a third set of that exercise? Maybe. But usually not. Two sets done the way I just described should trigger the specific adaptations you’re seeking. And you still have another exercise or two to complete next for that muscle group. Am I like Mentzer and think that if you do a third set, it’s going to be counterproductive? No. I don’t know if it will help your progress, but I don’t think it will hurt you if done in good form and with intense effort. You decide. One thing’s for sure: If you can’t make the set a highly focused, max effort work set, move on.

Once you hit failure, should you do assisted (sometimes called “forced”) reps? Or a drop set, where you reach failure then quickly lower the amount of weight and grind out one to three more reps before hitting failure again? These techniques can be helpful, but they stress your nervous system a lot. I would suggest pushing beyond failure for two to three sets maximum across the entire workout. On days where you’re feeling a bit stressed, don’t push past failure. And if you have someone assisting you with forced reps, make sure they don’t jump in before you reach failure. Make sure they force you to do the work. It’s a fine line between spotting someone to ensure they don’t get stuck in a dangerous position during a lift and getting someone to help you with forced reps.

Spotting someone in the weight room is a skill—it’s not brain surgery but there is a right and a wrong way to do it. On social media, you often come across videos of gym disasters, where people get stuck under the bench press or squat bar because they were too shy to ask for a spot. There are, however, a nearly equal number of gym disaster videos of young kids who were not able to pull the bar off their dad’s chest because they are too weak. Avoid all of this by making sure anyone you ask to help you is (1) strong enough to help with the amount of weight you’re using and (2) understands that you need to do the majority of the work. They are there to help keep you safe (again, especially on bench presses or squats where getting stuck can be dangerous), but not hinder your progress. Tell them: “I’ll let you know when to help but don’t touch the weight until I say.” And if they check their phone during your work sets, find a new training partner!
REST DURATION BETWEEN SETS

Just as I listed above, take one to two minutes off between warm-up sets, and two to five minutes between work sets, depending on repetition range. Typically, people rest longer (3–5 minutes) between work sets of compound exercises than between work sets of isolation exercises (90 seconds to 3 minutes). Some people adhere to the clock for between set rest, others go by feel. You decide. I use the clock to get a sense of how my subjective “Okay, I’m ready for another set” sense matches up with various time ranges. Just don’t talk, text, or scroll too much between sets. Stay focused, get the training done and get out.
Recovery tips
Then there’s the rest that comes after your resistance training session.

Great things happen for your health during your resistance training sessions but the really big benefits—the actual changes in your muscles, connective tissues, and brain—occur during the two to four days afterward, mostly while you sleep. [^93] The protocols provided elsewhere in this book will help you get your sleep right and your nutrition and stress control right—all of which support recovery from, and adaptation to, exercise. You do not need to overhaul your sleep schedule or diet just because you resistance train. It is true that if you do a particularly hard workout, you may find you need a bit more sleep on subsequent nights, but in general, resistance training has the effect of improving the quality of your sleep, not increasing your sleep duration needs.

Same with nutrition. Resistance training doesn’t massively change your nutritional needs. Assuming you are already eating in the manner I describe in chapter 4—meaning you strive to eat about 1 gram of quality protein per pound of lean body weight daily, as well as plenty of vegetables, some fruit, unprocessed starches, and healthy fats.

It is true that if you are actively seeking to gain muscle, you’ll need to eat more calories than you burn each day, but not by much—200 to 400 calories more than your maintenance calories is fine. [^94] The old-school practice of bulking up by eating many more calories than you need is just not healthy—and brings with it a lot of body fat that you’ll be trying to lose later. [^95] I suggest you don’t go that route. Provided you are not undernourished in calories or protein, you’ll make progress with resistance training. Keep in mind as you gain more muscle and/or lose fat, your caloric needs change—fortunately in a way that lets you eat the same or more while staying lean or even getting leaner. Muscle tissue is metabolically demanding, which means it burns more calories than fat tissue, which is just one of the many benefits of resistance training.

There is a formula for determining your maintenance calorie needs per day, or what is called your basal metabolic rate (BMR). That’s how many calories you should eat each day to maintain your current body weight if you did no physical activity whatsoever.

The formula is called the Katch-McArdle formula. [^96] It takes about five minutes to figure out, and it’s very easy to do. It requires a few other simple calculations first, which I’ll walk you through.
Determine your body weight (BW) in kilograms:
• The formula uses kilograms so if you’re used to thinking about weight in pounds and not kilograms, first divide your body weight (BW) in pounds by 2.2 to get your weight in kilograms.
• For example, I weigh 220 pounds, so 220/2.2 = 100 kilograms.
Calculate your lean body mass (LBM):
• Multiply your BW in kilograms by 1 minus your body fat percentage as a decimal.
• For example, I weigh 220 pounds (100 kg) and am about 10% body fat, so my LBM is approximately 100 × (1 – 0.10) = 90 kilograms.
• To estimate your body fat percentage, these online resources can help you figure that out: Men: https://athleanx.com/articles/body-fat-percentage-men
• Women: https://ultimateperformance.com/your-goal/fat-loss/female-fat-loss/womens-body-fat-percentage-in-pictures/
• There are more precise methods to measure body fat percentage, but they can be costly. This works pretty well, and is available at no cost.
Calculate your basal metabolic rate (BMR):
• Katch-McArdle equation: BMR = 370 + (21.6 × LBM in kilograms).
• So for me: BMR = 370 + (21.6 × 90) = 370 + (1944) = 2,314 calories per day, my BMR.
Multiply your BMR by an activity multiplier to account for how active you are throughout the day:
• Sedentary (no exercise at all): BMR × 1.2
• Lightly active (e.g., walking 7,000–10,000 steps): BMR × 1.375
• Moderately active (e.g., same as lightly active, plus yoga, “easy” cardio): BMR × 1.55
• Very active (e.g., walking 7K–10K steps, effortful resistance training or cardio): BMR × 1.725
• Extremely active (e.g., same as very active but two-a-day-workouts): BMR × 1.9

I’ll add one comment on estimating your activity levels from sports performance expert Andy Galpin. Based on his experience training hundreds of clients in reaching their fitness goals, Andy notes that people are typically far less active than they think. For example, most who rate themselves “very active” are actually moderately active. He recommends that people select the activity category below the one they think they fall into if they’re interested in losing weight.

I don’t do resistance training and cardio on the same days, but I try to get seven thousand to ten thousand steps in every day, and I resistance train three times a week and do some form of cardio three days a week.

Occasionally, I will resistance train or run, and then also go for a hike. That constitutes extremely active but it’s too rare an occurrence. Also, given Andy’s recommendation, I’ll consider myself “very active” and therefore multiply my basal metabolic maintenance calories (2,314 calories) by 1.725 = 3,991.65 calories… and I round that up to 4,000 calories per day.
I naturally tend to eat less on days I don’t exercise, so for that day, I multiply 2,314 by 1.375 = 3,181.75 calories.

Voila! I need about 4,000 calories per day on my training days and about 3,000 calories per day on my non-training days. Do I neurotically count every calorie? No. Truth be told, I probably eat about 3,500 calories on training days, and about 3,000 calories on days I don’t train.

Should you count calories? Maybe, but not every day and certainly not forever. I suggest figuring out your basal metabolic maintenance calories, what you’re consuming now, and what changes you need to make, and then stick to that revised plan most of the time.

After you’ve completed the simple formula above, a great tool to track what you’re eating is the Carbon app developed by Layne Norton, PhD, who is an expert in training and nutrition. (Carbon is a sponsor of my podcast because I believe it to be a terrific product.) Another option is the Cal AI app. Both make it very easy to enter what you eat and the apps then do all the calculations of calories, as well as macronutrients like protein, fats, and carbohydrates. Each carries a nominal cost, but it is very easy to use. Personally, I don’t like to count calories every day, but I use the Carbon app for periods of time to see how I’m doing.

If you want to lose weight, eating 300 to 500 fewer calories than you burn daily is the best way to go. By resistance training while in this caloric deficit, you’re better able to spare lean muscle and preferentially lose fat. [^97] This is further helped by making sure you’re eating a protein-rich diet, despite eating 300 to 500 fewer calories. In short, resistance training and a good diet are two of the most effective and durable paths to body recomposition—a fancy term for “gaining muscle and losing fat,” as opposed to simply losing weight.
Pre-training and post-training nutrition

I prefer to resistance train early in the morning or midafternoon, and I consistently have my best workouts when I have not eaten anything in the hours before I begin. I like to wake up, get sunlight, hydrate, caffeinate, then train, and then eat afterward, but some people just can’t do that. They feel weak, tired, hungry, or nauseous if they train on an empty stomach. But I know myself well. If 10:00 or 11:00 a.m. rolls around and I haven’t eaten, I need to ingest some calories before training. That’s usually a few scoops of whey protein, a small bowl of oatmeal, a piece of fruit, and some nuts. Nothing fancy. Or two to three eggs, instead of the whey. You’ll have to experiment to see what works best for you. If you eat before you train, ideally give yourself at least an hour to digest your food before you begin.

After resistance training, your body is primed to convert any food you consume into energy to burn at a very high rate, so it can replace glycogen you used during the workout. [^98] That does not mean you should gorge on pastries or pizza after training. Unless you’re deliberately low-carb or keto, the meal following a resistance training workout ideally should include both natural sugars (a few pieces of fruit) and starchy complex carbohydrates (such as rice, potatoes, bread, pasta, or oatmeal) to replenish glycogen stores in your liver and muscles. It should also include some quality protein (such as whey, beef, chicken, fish, turkey, or eggs).

This meal doesn’t have to be complicated. The enzymes that facilitate restocking of glycogen are upregulated after resistance training, [^99] and you direct more of the amino acids coming from the protein you eat into your muscle tissue after resistance training too, [^100] so it’s a good idea to eat within the three hours after training. [^101] BUT, contrary to the lore in the 1990s, if you don’t eat in this window, it’s not the end of the world! As long as you don’t eat far too few calories, you’ll still make progress. You’ll likely recover faster if you do eat in this window, but follow your hunger cues. There is a lot more to say about nutrition and training. Far more than can be covered here, but I provide a few more tips below, and even more in chapter 4.
Hydration

Drink water before, during, and after a workout, especially on hot days or if you tend to sweat a lot. I cover hydration later in chapter 4 as well. Yes, there is a protocol for how to hydrate properly, as this is one of the most undervalued tools for mental and physical performance.
Supplements

You do not need supplements to make progress with your resistance training. What’s most important is that you train hard, get enough sleep, and eat right. If you want to explore supplements, however, there are two that have been shown to increase strength and hypertrophy: creatine monohydrate and whey protein.

Creatine brings more water into your muscles, enhancing training capacity and recovery ability, which thus makes you stronger. It also can have some positive effects on brain function, [^102] especially after mild sleep deprivation. [^103] I take five to ten grams of creatine monohydrate daily, as a powder dissolved in water. You can take it any time of day, with or without food. Any reputable brand with third-party testing and that is “Certified for Sport” is fine. I have seen no evidence that creatine harms your kidneys [^104] or makes your hair fall out, [^105] which is what some online claims say. It’s normal to gain a few pounds of water-in-the-muscles weight with regular creatine use. If you stop taking it, you urinate out that extra fluid.

Whey protein is simply a high-quality, easily digested protein. It’s convenient and cost-effective when compared to other quality proteins. It doesn’t have many other micronutrients like meat or eggs do, however, so I wouldn’t make whey protein your only quality protein source. I drink one to two scoops of whey protein mixed with water once or twice a day, which equates to 20 to 80 grams of protein (it’s about 20 g of protein per scoop). Along with the foods I eat, this helps me meet my daily protein goal. Without whey protein I find it challenging to eat about 1 gram per pound of lean body weight each day.

The other supplement worth mentioning in the context of resistance training is caffeine, which has been shown to improve exercise performance when 100 to 400 milligrams is consumed about thirty minutes prior to and even during exercise. [^106] That’s about one to four cups of coffee, depending on the brew strength and size of the serving. Not everyone can or should consume caffeine, however. It makes some people anxious. I personally love caffeine and tolerate it very well, so I drink a cup or two of black coffee and/or a yerba maté about thirty minutes before resistance workouts.

A lot of people are into energy drinks these days as pre- and intra-workout energy sources. I will occasionally drink an energy drink (Jocko Go or Gorilla Mind—I know, wild names!—are the ones I like best for taste and effect) before and during a workout, but not every time. If I am facing a particularly challenging leg workout I tend to make my own pre-workout by drinking (or taking) 200 milligrams of caffeine and alpha-GPC (300–900 mg). I discuss alpha-GPC and other compounds more in chapter 6. Just remember, if you’re working out in the evening, drinking caffeine beforehand will really disrupt your sleep.

There are a few other supplements which have been shown to improve exercise performance—like Rhodiola rosea, which can reduce fatigue during training, [^107] but I consider it a distant fourth place to the three mentioned already.

But I want to reiterate: You do not need supplements to make progress resistance training. Focus on training properly! Then focus on recovery, meaning letting the adaptations you stimulated in the gym actually occur by getting proper sleep and nutrition. That is what really moves the needle.
A week off every twelve to sixteen (or even ten to twelve) weeks

I attribute taking a week off from resistance training every three to four months or so as one of the main reasons I have been able to make regular progress in resistance training over the last thirty-five years. I know that sounds crazy, and that it runs counter to much of the “no days off” advice seen online, but I am convinced it’s the way to go, for three reasons.
First, it gives your joints and your mind a chance to reset. Any nagging aches or residual muscle soreness tend to go away during that week off, and you come back feeling reset.

Second, most people make actual progress during the week off. Training-induced stress is cumulative; when we train and recover between workouts, we get stronger and can manage more reps and/or more weight in perfect form from week to week, but not all our bodily tissues adapt at the same rate. By the time we are eight, nine, or even fourteen weeks into training since our last week off, we tend to have a harder time recovering from workouts. Taking a week off lets everything catch up, and lets you come back stronger.

Third, it’s common that after twelve to sixteen weeks of training we feel less motivated to keep training hard. The relatively low frequency of resistance training I recommend in this program—just three times per week—usually staves off boredom but some people do start to lose steam after ten or more weeks of training. If you find yourself dragging yourself to the gym, and you’re more interested in texting than training once you’re there, take a week off, and come back. That usually does the trick. You’ll be more energetic when you do.

Keep in mind, too, that sometimes we are just forced to take a week off because life says we have to! I don’t think training when you’re sick is a good idea, and it gets others sick, too, so please stay out of the gym until you’re better! Other times we are forced to take a week off because we have a major deadline or a family vacation or other demands. I personally like to train on vacations because it helps me get over jet lag when I travel, but you may feel like it’s a waste of time. It’s a matter of choice, and how you view vacation.

Regardless of whether your week off is due to a cold or pre-planned for the end of a twelve to sixteen week stretch of training, or simply because a work deadline hits, don’t worry about it causing a setback. It’s part of the process. Just get back to training (properly) after that week off.
COMMON QUESTIONS
Does it matter what day I begin this sequence
No. Start it on Sunday or Tuesday or whenever you like. What’s important is to follow the sequence.

You listed abdominals/core as “required” but neck and forearms as optional. Why? And am I supposed to train neck and abdominals/core and forearms the same way I train other muscles, with progressive overload, to failure, et cetera

Some people need to work on their forearms—and their grip strength—and others don’t, for a variety of reasons. It could be genetics, or because that second group targets their forearms and grip strength with plenty of work from deadlifts, pull-ups, rows, and similar movements. Grip strength is a correlate of longevity but not a cause. It’s also one of the things that starts to wane as we age. I like training forearms when I train shoulders and arms, and just for three to four sets of flexor and/or extensor movements (see protocolsbook.com/videos for examples). Use higher rep ranges, say twelve to thirty reps—no need to train forearms with lower reps and heavy weight. You’ll get that indirectly from your heavier pulling movements when you train your back, such as chin-ups or rows.

Abdominals are a specific set of muscles in your midsection and your “core” includes a lot more than just these. I suggest you train your abs and core one to two times per week. Endless crunches are not the way to go. There are better options to train these muscles. And some let you train your forearms and strengthen your grip, and let you get in a great stretch too, all at once. Like hanging from a bar and doing knee raises, then progressing over time to hanging chair sits and L-sits, where you hold your legs straight out, parallel to the floor, and eventually hanging pikes, where you bring your shins up to the bar. You don’t just leap into pikes, by the way; you work toward these with the exercises above, and everyone—yes, everyone (men and women)—I have taken through this progression has eventually been able to do multiple sets of three to five reps of hanging pikes! They were surprised, but I was not. Your body is amazing in how it will adapt if you give it the right stimulus, and the right recovery. (Oh, and I know three to five reps is not ten, but when you reach that number you will have a very strong core and grip!)

Other reasons to train your core: It’s vital for posture and back health, and it will help your resistance and other fitness training. Six-pack abs are the consequence of having low enough body fat to see the contour of the abdominals. You don’t get that from training alone. But abs and other muscles of your core react to progressive overload just like any other muscle (here too, see protocolsbook.com/videos for examples).

Neck exercises are the least performed of any exercises in any gym, but they are so important! Your neck is your upper spine, and a strong neck is crucial for posture. It also helps to keep your shoulders uninjured. Also, done right they won’t give you a huge neck—or (oxymoronically) the “no-neck” look. Women and men who train their neck properly can avoid that look if they want to, and yet can still enjoy the better posture and facial tone that work can bring, as the neck and face muscles both activate during these exercises. For wide-shouldered men, balanced neck development is crucial to avoid appearing as if your head is too small for your body! This will be of great aesthetic and structural benefit. Neck training is simple to do safely and effectively once you know how, and requires little or no equipment. I include several examples also at protocolsbook.com/videos.

Everyone should be sure to train their rear deltoid muscles—small muscles on the back of the shoulders that, when made sufficiently strong, greatly improve posture and shoulder stability. There is a way to train this muscle along with other muscles of the middle back that will also help make your default posture more upright. The exercise is called a “face pull,” and no, it does not involve attaching weights to your face or jaw. You do them during your “shoulders and arms” resistance training day, using exercise bands or a cable machine. I have a video of the person who popularized these, Jeff Cavaliere from AthleanX, teaching me the proper form at protocolsbook.com/videos.
What if something comes up and I have to miss a workout, what then

I address this in Exercise Protocol 3, because the resistance training outlined here is part of a larger program. In the meantime, know that you have a fair degree of flexibility, and you can move a workout forward or back a day if needed.
Can I still play sports and do other activities

Of course. You’ll be stronger for it. And the relatively low volume of sets in this program means you won’t be sore all the time. (Again, soreness is zero indication of an effective workout—it does not mean you effectively stimulated specific hypertrophy or strength adaptations.) Please don’t add additional resistance training work or CrossFit workouts and the like until you’ve tried this program, but tennis, Pilates, hiking, yoga, archery, golf, soccer, et cetera, and being active with house and yard work is encouraged. Most people nowadays are too sedentary. More movement is nearly always better than less. And of course, cardiovascular training is key. I discuss that next.
EXERCISE PROTOCOL 3 Do Cardiovascular Training Three Times per Week
WHAT TO DO

• Elevate your heart rate for anywhere from six to seventy-five minutes, three times per week. Plan three sessions, each focused on stimulating a different specific adaptation: a long, a medium, and a brief cardiovascular workout, scaling the intensity inversely with the duration of each session. That means the long cardio workout should be of low intensity, the brief cardio workout should be of high intensity. Here is how to incorporate cardio into the overall program:
• Day 1: Cardiovascular training, 45–75 minutes (low intensity/long duration)
• Day 2: Resistance training (legs: calves, quadriceps, hamstrings, glutes)
• Day 3: Rest day
• Day 4: Resistance training (torso: chest, back, abdominals/core; optional neck)
• Day 5: Cardiovascular training, 25–30 minutes (moderate intensity/moderate duration)
• Day 6: Cardiovascular training, 6–17 minutes (high intensity/brief duration)
• Day 7: Resistance training (shoulders, biceps, triceps, abdominals/core; optional forearms and/or neck)

The first cardio workout each week marks the first day of the foundational fitness program schedule. It should be relatively low intensity, and long duration. And it should be continuous. Your goal is to sustain a steady output of effort for forty-five to seventy-five minutes without any pauses except perhaps to drink some water or wait for a stoplight to change so you can cross the street. This falls into the category of classic endurance work. The primary adaptation you’re stimulating with this workout is to increase your heart’s stroke volume, which is the amount of blood your heart pumps with each beat. This means the heart can pump more blood per beat, and thus does not have to beat as fast to deliver the same amount of oxygen. The consequences of that for your health are manifold, including a lower resting heart rate when not exercising. [^108] This workout also stimulates a number of metabolic pathways related to utilizing fat for fuel and for vascular growth and even lymphatic health. [^109] It indirectly improves mood and sleep too. [^110]

The challenge of this workout resides in its duration, not its intensity, and for many people the most challenging aspect is refraining from going faster and harder as they complete it. The forty-five to seventy-five minute duration is intentionally broad. In fact, if you’re out of shape when starting this program, I suggest you begin with just fifteen to twenty minutes, and add a few minutes to that each week, until you’re doing forty-five to seventy-five minutes of continuous movement. In my observation, most people find that sixty minutes is about the upper limit of their psychological tolerance for this sort of exercise, unless they really love the activity or it’s made social, like a hike or bike ride with family or friends. In any case, your goal pace throughout should be such that you can just barely hold a conversation. It’s quite all right if you must pause your speech here and there to catch your breath, but the idea is to exert yourself at a level that, were you to push yourself any faster or harder, holding a conversation would be impossible.

Another way to calibrate to that goal pace is to push as hard as you can while still breathing in and out only through your nose. No mouth breathing whatsoever, unless you are talking. As soon as you feel you have to gasp to get air through your mouth, you know you’re pushing too hard.

In the language of percentage of maximum heart rate this cardio session is done at 60 to 70 percent of your maximum heart rate (HR), but ideally closer to 70 percent. Your max HR can be estimated by this formula: 220 – your age = your approximate max HR. That’s not a perfect measurement but it’s close, and for most it’s more than sufficient to use here. If you want to be more precise about it, max HR is better approximated by the following formula: for men, you take 208 beats per minute – (0.7 × your age in years); and for women, it’s 206 beats per minute – (0.88 × your age in years). [^111] Once you have determined your approximate max HR, multiply that by 0.6 and 0.7 to get the lower and upper range, respectively, of your target heart rate for this cardio session. I’ve shared this formula because some people like to use an HR monitor while training to be sure they stay in that target HR zone. I prefer to use the “upper limit of effort while maintaining nasal breathing” approach, because whenever I have measured my HR while running and restricting myself to nasal breathing, it lands at about 70 percent (+/–5 percent) of my max HR. I have nothing against HR monitors. I just prefer not to use one when doing this workout. I like to let my mind wander or to listen to a book or podcast or music but if you like tracking your HR in real time, go for it.

A few other things to consider for this workout: Some people refer to this as Zone 2 cardio, which is a term that describes the intensity of the exercise with regard to heart rate training zones. But on that scale, I consider it more Zone ⅔ because it’s done at the high end of Zone 2 and the low end of Zone 3. [^112]

Ideally you would get outside to do this workout so that you’re getting all the benefits that come with being outdoors. This raises the issue of what type of exercise is best for this. That’s an easy one to answer. Select any activity you can do for the specified duration and intensity without getting hurt. That means do what is safe for your joints, works for your skill level, doesn’t stress any of your injuries, and can be completed in safe conditions. I love running and much prefer doing it outside on a trail or city streets to all other forms of cardio, but many people loathe running, or it hurts their knees, or it’s not safe for them to run in a given area. You don’t have to run! You can opt for cycling, or use the elliptical machine or a stair climber, or hike with a weight vest or a rucksack or, heck, even a backpack with a one-gallon jug of water in it. The possibilities are nearly infinite, and many of these cost very little. If I don’t run, I’ll sometimes swim laps in a pool or swim parallel to shore in the ocean. If the weather is bad, I’ll occasionally run on a treadmill or use a stationary bike.

Pick your poison and deliver it slow and steady for forty-five to seventy-five minutes. Many people find this workout meditative and learn to enjoy it. While you can of course go longer than seventy-five minutes, remember you’re training your legs the next day.

The second cardio workout each week is done three days after your leg workout (day five of the program). By then, your legs should be feeling mostly or completely recovered. This second cardio workout should be moderately fast-paced. It should have you breathing fairly hard but not gasping for air or needing to stop to recover. I suggest you start with five minutes of low-intensity movement to warm up and then shift to twenty-five to thirty minutes of “work” where your heart rate is kept between about 75 and 85 percent of your maximum heart rate.
Using the heart rate training zones, this workout falls in the high Zone 3 and low Zone 4 range.

Notably, although this workout is more intense than the first cardio session, it generally leaves you feeling energized and focused for many hours afterward. The key is to not push overly hard at any one time of that approximately twenty-five to thirty minutes. You want to stay roughly in that “75 to 85 percent of max HR” range. That said, it’s perfectly all right to move between high and low within this range by pushing harder at times, and pulling back at times. Say, for example, you’re climbing a hill or you’re just feeling strong on your bike for a stretch and want to push yourself. Your pace and your heart rate don’t have to be perfectly constant throughout. Remember: It’s not a sprint! You don’t want to overly tax your body. The third cardio workout is the one that is intense. Luckily, it’s brief too.

The third cardio workout each week lands four days following your leg workout. If you still have a bit of residual leg soreness, no big deal: Proceed anyway. Some people refer to this type of workout as Zone 5 training or HIIT (high-intensity interval training), but I like to refer to it as “max heart rate training” or simply “intense cardio” because there are non-interval ways to do it, and—for reasons that will become clear in a minute—getting your heart pumping near your maximum heart rate is highly beneficial.

There are a few variations in the “classic” versions of this workout. All begin with five to ten minutes of warming up at an easy to moderate pace. HIIT has you modulating between near-all-out efforts that put you at 90 to 95 percent of your max HR, interspersed with bouts of lower intensity effort where you let your HR fall a bit before repeating the sequence. [^113] Another approach is to start at an easy effort and build in a continuous and progressive manner—for example, increasing the level of resistance to your effort (think: increasing treadmill speed and incline)—until your effort plateaus, or starts to drop. (That actually mirrors how a VO2 max test, a measure of fitness and endurance, is conducted.) There are many ways to do max heart rate training but the total time spent at near-all-out effort is always pretty brief: as short as about six minutes, and up to about sixteen minutes. Either works for this third cardio session.

What form of exercise you choose can vary. For example, you could hop on an assault bike—those stationary bikes with a fan and handles that you pump forward and back while you pedal. You’ll soon realize that the fan is there to increase the resistance, not just to cool you down. Or you could use a stationary bike that lets you adjust the resistance of the pedals. You could also go sprint at a track or on a trail, or swim in a pool. The important thing is to do something in which you can really exert yourself without getting injured.

A “fun” HIIT session is this: brief five- to ten-minute warm-up, then pedal (or run, row, or swim, etc.) as hard and fast as you can for thirty seconds, then rest or slow down for sixty seconds, then another thirty seconds of all-out effort, then back again to sixty seconds of rest or low effort, and so on, for a total of six to twelve rounds of alternations. I do this on the assault bike once a week. I love-hate it.

You will quickly realize that with each round of all-out effort it gets tougher and tougher to recover, such that by rounds six to twelve, those sixty seconds of rest will seem to go by extremely fast. There is actually a neuroscientific basis for the warping of time perception we experience under stress that I discuss in the next chapter. The good news is, even though this workout is intense, the whole thing, including the warm-up, only takes about twenty-five minutes. At the end, you will feel fatigued, but remarkably, within five to ten minutes after stopping you will likely feel extra energized from all the adrenaline and norepinephrine you generated in your body and brain. [^114] You will also have provided a great stimulus to improve your VO2 max, and max HR, the importance of which I cover below.
Other options for this workout include the Cooper test, where you see how far you can go (run, swim, cycle, etc.) in twelve minutes of steady, hard effort. [^115] That is a “fun” one too.

Or you can try to run your best mile time. This is something performance coach, author, and former elite runner Steve Magness has emphasized as being a terrific correlate of VO2 max. [^116] It’s one of my favorite workouts. Here is how to do it properly:

First find a 400-meter track. Start by warming up with an easy jog of four to six laps slowly interspersing the occasional faster-paced 100 meters—not all out but just quickening your pace to about 60 to 70 percent of your subjective “run for your life” speed. Perhaps do that on one straight-track segment between turns on each warm-up lap. Once you feel properly warmed up, run four laps (which is 1,600 meters—about 9 meters shy of 1 mile). It’s a skill to run the mile and pace everything just right for your best time. But you’re not aiming to be a competitive miler here. So set out at a pace you can maintain for three laps—about 85 percent of “running for your life” speed, then push it harder on the last lap, or 95 percent of “running for your life” speed. The key is to pace yourself so you’re not sprinting laps one to three and then forced to walk or jog the remainder. It can take a bit of practice but within a few weeks you’ll know the pace to take for each lap. Almost everyone likes to really push the final 200 meters or so.

I test my approximate best mile time about once every two months lately. I’m not training to be a competitive miler but it’s nice to have one version of the short intense cardio workout where I can track my progress across the year. I doubt I’ll beat my best time from high school ever again, but it’s fun to have an “a bit faster than last month” run. My goal is to maintain or reduce my mile time each time I run it.

And there is the Norwegian 4×4, if you want to try it. [^117] That’s where you warm up, and then run, bike, or row hard for four minutes, then rest or slow down for four minutes. Repeat this cycle for a total of four work-rest rounds.

As you can see with all these examples, the exact work-to-rest ratio and total time can vary dramatically, and yet all can be effective. What’s key is that during the work periods, you’re truly working hard. That is because, during the rest periods, you’re allowing enough time for recovery so that you can again come back to a truly hard effort. Don’t be overly caught up in the exact protocols. You can alter them if you like and still get the same results.

I’m recommending three different types of cardio training sessions every week because this variation is typically what delivers the best results over time for improving your VO2 max. We’re trying to balance duration and intensity in this program. It’s best to emphasize both. You want longer moderate efforts and you want brief and very intense efforts. And while the shorter, intense efforts are extremely effective (and time efficient), they take longer to recover from compared to the longer, moderate efforts. Given that you’re also balancing this cardio training with the resistance training, a blend of longer/lower, moderate, and brief/high intensity cardio training sessions is what works best for results across the board.
HOW IT WORKS

The cardio workouts described above each help trigger beneficial adaptations. They all increase your heart’s efficiency in delivering blood (and thus oxygen and vital nutrients) to the rest of the body. [^118] They trigger capillary growth in your muscles, which allows more oxygen to move through these vessels during all activities. [^119] They stimulate an increase in the number, size, and efficiency of your mitochondria, the energy producing organelles in our cells known to be critical for preventing chronic disease and premature aging. Further, they all acutely elevate levels of the catecholamines: dopamine, epinephrine, and norepinephrine. [^120] Also, because they rely on a mixture of aerobic (oxygen dependent) and anaerobic (oxygen independent) processes, cardio of the types in this program increases metabolic flexibility, or your body’s ability to rely on different fuel sources for energy. And that’s just a small sampling of the many beneficial adaptations. [^121]

The extent to which brief, high-intensity or longer, lower-intensity cardio triggers these different adaptations varies, but there is also synergy between them. [^122] Those brief, intense cardio training sessions will allow you to move faster but with less effort on your long and medium cardio days, not unlike how getting stronger with low repetition heavy sets in the gym equates to you being able to move more weight on your higher repetition sets once you get stronger.

So, while people often debate which form of cardiovascular exercise is best for overall health and longevity, that’s not the lens through which to look at it. I suggest a practical lens. (And you know by now, I don’t believe in any best type of exercise; only the best way to structure an effective exercise program.) For instance, consider that your one-mile time is a good reflection of your VO2 max. [^123] Does that mean you should only do one mile distances for cardio? No. In fact, whether you’re a competitive miler or simply using the one-mile time test as a fun workout and barometer of your VO2 max, doing some longer/lower, moderate, and brief/high intensity cardio workouts across the week is how to get faster at the mile.

In science we love to isolate variables, so people have done the “which cardio exercise is best?” experiment. That research made clear that if you have to choose one type, you want to opt for brief/high intensity cardio rather than, say, three thirty- to forty-five-minute Zone ⅔ sessions. [^124] But doing a mix of durations and intensities is recommended, and for the reasons mentioned above, it meshes well with your resistance training. A Zone ⅔ jog or hike for an hour the day before you train your legs with weights is no problem. Sprinting the day after leg training to failure? Not a good idea. The injury risk is too high.

Doing these three cardio training sessions also means you’re logging a total of about two hours per week of cardio. Considering the immediate and long-term health benefits, that’s a great return on investment.

We hear all the time about “fitness” and it reflects many things. But from a health perspective consider that two studies—one published in 2018 and another in 2022—both showed essentially the same thing, which is that as you move from the lowest to the higher tiers of cardiorespiratory fitness (one measure of that is your VO2 max), your mortality risk drops. [^125] These are meaningful shifts in life expectancy too. One of the studies states, “Those with the highest fitness had roughly five times lower mortality than the least fit.”

Resistance training is less about cardiorespiratory fitness, but its effects in maintaining (or increasing) muscle mass and bone density, promoting cognitive function and healthy body recomposition, make a combination of resistance training and cardio training two of the three vital interlocking puzzle pieces for excellent physical health.
COMMON QUESTIONS
Does doing three cardio training sessions per week prevent you from building muscle? And does resistance training harm my cardio efforts
