To be clear: If your goal is purely to put on as much muscle as possible, or to do an endurance event like a half marathon or marathon as fast as possible, there are better training programs for those specific goals. When splitting your time across both building muscle and building endurance, there’s going to be a performance trade-off. You can’t maximize for both at the same time because of so-called interference effects. [^126]

That said, for vitality, health, longevity, aesthetics, and all-around fitness, you want to do both resistance training and cardio training. Research indicates that the interference effects are minimal when done on separate days at the duration and intensities similar to those in this foundational program. [^127]
What if I play a sport

If you’re training for a competition or a race, or you play a sport like soccer or tennis or basketball, and you play hard for an hour or more one to two times per week, the program here is still great. You may want to do the lower number of work sets, and you’ll really need to tend to your recovery and nutrition by making sure you get enough hours of quality sleep and calories—including, yes, enough quality protein, but also starches and fats.

Again, the program here will get you the most all-around fit as possible at any age. That does not mean you won’t gain strength and muscle—you will. You will also burn fat. You’ll increase your endurance too. And once you learn how different exercises impact your body, you can emphasize some and reduce others, per the suggestions I describe in this protocol. Exercise done correctly is very potent in that way. Assuming you pay attention to the points I make about recovery too—that is, eat well and sleep well—I’m certain you’ll achieve remarkable results with this program.
What if I haven’t slept well, should I train or not

If you are healthy, and you happen to have had a bad night’s sleep—by which I mean only one to two hours less sleep than usual—then try to stick with your workout. There is a growing amount of data that say it can help offset some of the short-term cognitive disturbances from sleep loss. [^128]

Just be careful not to push too hard in the gym (or in life) after a poor night’s sleep as injuries happen more often when people have not slept enough. [^129] And don’t make it a regular thing to get less than enough sleep, and expect to remedy that with exercise. You’ll end up sick, injured, or both. Maybe do some non-sleep deep rest (NSDR) (see Sleep Protocol 8) and then push through the workout. If you have had a really bad night’s sleep for two or more nights in a row, for whatever reason, I suggest you get back on track with your sleep before exercising again. Consider some deliberate heat exposure (sauna or a hot bath, for example), and if you feel you must exercise, try a restorative activity, like stretching, light yoga, or just walking.
Is it better to eat before or after training

There is no clear rule here. Personally, I prefer to train in the morning on an empty stomach. Figure out what works for you. It may be best to eat prior to training if you wake up hungry and you know that hunger will distract you during your workout, or you get dizzy or nauseous training on an empty stomach. Some people may find that eating about sixty to ninety minutes prior to exercise gives them an energy boost without the discomfort of feeling full. It’s highly individual. Experiment with your timing of your workouts and meals.
If I miss a day of cardio or resistance training, should I change the weekly schedule

It’s hard to answer this one because… it depends. However, I would not change the order of your resistance or cardio training sessions across the week because the schedule starts to fall like dominoes, and it’s hard to get back on track. But maybe something comes up and you can’t do the long, slow cardio day as planned. I would not recommend moving that workout to the same day you train legs. I would simply skip the long cardio day and train your legs on schedule. Skipping leg day is a bad idea. You do three days of cardio per week, so having to miss one every now and again is not a huge deal. But you only train your legs directly once a week, and done correctly as outlined above it creates major positive systemic shifts in your brain and body. So when people say, “Don’t skip leg day,” it’s not just about aesthetics. In fact, if I could only train once per week in the gym and do one cardio training session—not what I recommend, but if I had to—I would do leg day and I would do some sprints followed by light jogging four or five days later. That’s just to illustrate a point about the potency of those two workouts. I recommend the full program described in this chapter.

Let’s say you can’t do the moderate cardio training session for whatever reason. You could, in theory, shift it to immediately after your arms workout that same day. But remember, you’re scheduled to do the long, slow cardio session the very next day, and you don’t want your legs to feel like noodles when you wake up the following morning for leg day! So think ahead a bit about your recovery.

I suggest you stick to the schedule as best you can, missing days here and there or doubling up when there is no other option. Plan your workouts, follow through, and if people get curious about how you’re getting such great results, teach them the principles, or even better, share the program. No one owns this or any exercise program; they are all derivatives of each other anyway, and based on what science says works.
EXERCISE PROTOCOL 4 Incorporate Brief Mobility and Flexibility Work Two to Four Times per Week
WHAT TO DO
• Do four specific movements to improve your mobility, two to four times a week.

• Refer to the instructions below to target areas susceptible to injury as you do these movements. Wrist, back, knee, hip, and shoulder injuries are common. The movements described here will ensure mobility in these areas. They aren’t a guarantee against injuries, but they can help tremendously.
HOW IT WORKS

First, I’m not giving you yet another workout to do. The current program—about three hours a week of resistance training, about two hours of cardio—is not terribly time-consuming, considering the years (literally!) it can add to your life. Still, I acknowledge that people’s time is limited. That is why I suggest incorporating just a few minutes of mobility exercise two to four times per week. It can be done at the end of one of your other workouts, or any time of day really. It does not take long at all, only about ten minutes per session.

That might seem woefully inadequate to the mobility experts out there. I get it. I would love to add two thirty-minute mobility workouts to my own schedule but alas “my dance card is full,” as they say. I’m assuming yours is too.

The good news is that some aspects of the training suggested in the earlier protocols in this chapter are pro-mobility and pro-flexibility too. Remember the emphasis on using a full range of motion for resistance training sets, as described in Exercise Protocol 2? Doing that will not only build your strength and muscles but can also enhance your flexibility and mobility. In fact, some studies find that full-range resistance training can be as effective as static stretching, a type of stretching in which you hold a muscle in a stretched, or elongated, position and gradually deepen the stretch using body weight. Controlling the eccentric, or lowering, phase in full-range resistance training may be critical for this effect, which makes sense as that is when the muscle is elongating. [^130]

There are easy ways to get even more flexibility from resistance training too. In the resistance training video tutorials at protocolsbook.com/videos, I also emphasize some exercises that are hardest for a given muscle when the muscle is in the elongated, stretched position, as well as exercises where the tension is greatest when the muscle is in its shortened, contracted position. Consider a stiff-legged deadlift or similar variation for your hamstrings, glutes, and lower back—the so-called posterior chain. It involves holding a barbell or dumbbells and moving from standing to something resembling a toe-touch (or an attempt to) by lowering the weight under control toward the ground, and then standing up again. You can imagine the stretch to your hamstrings and lower back that movement provides if you use a full range of motion. Including some movements that are most challenging for a given muscle group when it is in the elongated position can help build flexibility and can help you remain “strong in any position,” which assists mobility too. [^131] Again, if any of this is confusing, I provide a gallery of movements to choose from at protocolsbook.com/videos.

I also hope you’ll include the direct mobility exercises that I describe below in your weekly routine but even if you don’t, by training the way I describe above, most people will improve their mobility, and flexibility too. We’re talking about the ability to touch your toes while keeping your legs straight or just slightly bent, to hang from a bar with no pain, to twist around to look behind you while seated in a chair, to sit in a deep squat for one to two minutes (and be able to stand up at the end!), and so on. You can develop those basic abilities through resistance training with a full range of motion, and focusing on the relevant muscles at all positions in each rep.
There are many great ways to improve mobility. Here I have created what I believe is the minimal effective dose of it. And if you want to do more mobility work, please do!
At least two to four times a week, take ten minutes and do the following four movements. You can do these most any place and at any time.
1 Deep sumo squat, torso twist, point, and look up
Set your feet a few inches wider than your shoulders, then squat down as far as you can.

Put your elbows against the insides of your knees and your palms and fingers together in “prayer” position, and push out gently with your elbows until you feel a stretch in your hips and inner thighs. Then raise one arm and, with your index finger, point directly up at the ceiling (or as high overhead as you can) while keeping your other elbow against the inside of your knee. Let your gaze follow your finger, which will naturally have you twist your torso and turn your neck to raise that arm. Look directly up at your index finger for three to ten seconds. Inhale and exhale.

Then put your arm down, reset to the first squat position with both elbows against the insides of your knees. Place your hands in prayer position for three to ten seconds, and then raise your other arm up to point at the ceiling. Twist your torso and look up at your index finger for three to ten seconds. Repeat three times for each side. You may have to stand up between sets. That is fine.

This is a great movement because it gets you squatting deep, it improves your thoracic spine and neck mobility, and you’ll also feel a decent stretch in your inner thighs and hips. It will also reveal if you have any asymmetries in your mobility (perhaps one side versus the other) which is common.
I demonstrate this movement here: protocolsbook.com/videos.
Note: If you can’t point and/or look all the way up to directly overhead, start by pointing and looking up at a lower angle. Gradually progress to pointing and looking directly overhead.
2 Get your knees behind your glutes, one at a time

This is one I learned from mobility expert Kelly Starrett whom I mentioned earlier in this chapter. Since it may not be easy for most people to envision, try this: Start in a standing lunge by placing one foot in front of you and the other foot behind you. Bend your front knee and keep your rear leg straight or a bit bent. Now nudge the foot in front of you slightly farther out. Bend that front knee more and focus on stretching the hip flexors at the top of your back leg. You may need to lean your torso back a bit to really feel the hip flexor stretch. Okay, notice the knee of your back leg is now behind your glutes? That is what I mean by “get your knee behind your glutes.” Slowly ease into this hip flexor stretch for ten to thirty seconds while exhaling. It’s fine to reach up and look overhead while doing this, as that will help extend the hip flexor, but keep your attention on the back leg. Your front leg is there for stability and you can bend it to provide more rear-placed-leg hip stretch. Repeat for each side three times. I demonstrate this movement here: protocolsbook.com/videos.

Next, you’re going to kneel on both knees. Then put one knee up in front of you (the foot of that same leg is thus flat on the ground). The shin of your rear leg is parallel to the ground. That means your back foot will be sole-facing-up. Place your hand on that raised front knee for stability and gently extend the back leg until you feel a stretch in your hip flexor. Again, think “I need to get my knee behind my glutes.” Keep your torso upright, your eyes forward or up, and even lean slightly back at the waist. Hold the stretch for ten to thirty seconds. Repeat three to four times. Don’t forget to breathe.
I demonstrate these movements here: protocolsbook.com/videos.

The reason to do this: Your hip flexors are located where your leg meets your pelvis. When you sit, your hip flexors are partially flexing. When you run, bike, or walk up a set of stairs, your hip flexors are repeatedly flexing as you bring your knee up and forward. Modern life has us flexing our hip flexors all the time. A key step toward good mobility is to make sure you can extend your hips. Hip extension is the opposite of hip flexion—it moves your knee away from the front of your pelvis, to a location behind you. Hence the directive here. Once you experience how good it feels during (and after!) this stretch, you’ll be looking for ways to do it more often.
3 Get into a reverse tabletop position

Sit on the floor with your feet in front of you, the soles of your feet and butt on the ground, and with your knees bent. Place your hands at your sides a few inches away from your hips, with your palms down. Turn your hands so your fingers point away from you out to each side.

See if you can slowly push your pelvis up so that the tops of your legs and torso are parallel to the floor, and your knees are at a 90 degree right angle. Many people find they can’t get into this “reverse tabletop” position for very long, if at all, but some can. See if you can hold that position for ten seconds.

If you can’t do this, practice doing this each week for three sets of however long you can hold it until you can easily remain in this position for ten seconds. Once you can do that, move to the following progression:

Sit on the floor with your feet in front of you, with the soles of your feet and butt on the ground, and your knees bent. Place your hands just behind your hips, with your palms down. Turn your hands so your fingers point backward. See if you can slowly push your pelvis up so that the tops of your legs and torso are parallel to the floor, and your knees are at a 90 degree right angle.

Once again, the goal is to get into the flat reverse tabletop position and hold for ten seconds. For some people this will take a while to achieve. For others it will be easy depending on your level of shoulder mobility. These movements are also great for wrist mobility, too, by the way.

Once that final “reverse tabletop” variation is achievable, then you can start to experiment SLOWLY with this next movement. Sit on the floor with your legs straight in front of you, heels on the ground and the soles of your feet facing forward. Place your hands flat on the ground just behind you, with your fingers pointed backward. Keep them there as you gently and slowly scoot your glutes forward. Remember, your hands stay flat on the ground and fixed in place. Keep scooting forward until you feel a stretch in your biceps and shoulders. Exhale, and see if you can ease into it another centimeter or so. Once you can extend your shoulders back behind you with the edges of your hands touching, you are getting to quite mobile shoulder status.

The reason to do this: Tight shoulders can arise from many sources, but often there will be people who can raise their arms to the front or to the side without issue but who don’t have the mobility to raise their arms up behind them, meaning they don’t have much shoulder extension mobility. This is made worse by desk work, and the chin-down/forward-leaning posture that is nearly ubiquitous nowadays, thanks to excessive amounts of time texting and scrolling on our phones. Shoulder tightness and neck and back pain are often linked too. Improving your shoulder extension mobility is straightforward. It just requires a willingness to work through these progressions.

Wrist, back, knee, hip, and shoulder injuries are super common and many can be avoided by a quality strength training program and by including some basic mobility exercises like the ones in this protocol. Some quick movements you can incorporate in your routine are the “face pulls,” which strengthen these and other areas, as well as neck training a few times a week, as described in Exercise Protocol 2 and shown at protocolsbook.com/videos. You will be amazed at how strong, mobile, and stable your shoulders, neck, and upper back will be if you do.

Do not push too fast when it comes to mobility work! Work through the progressions listed above over the course of months or more. Make it painless but deliberate, and you will build and maintain much greater shoulder, hip, knee, back, and wrist mobility.
4 Practice the Founder pose

The final mobility exercise is the Founder pose, made popular by chiropractor Eric Goodman, who has served as a conditioning coach for numerous top athletes in sports ranging from cycling to surfing to water polo. I was referred to his work by friends who previously had back pain and shoulder pain, and who sit a lot of the day. “You have to try this thing called Founder pose,” I kept hearing. Mind you, in my role, I hear that about a thousand times per day about a variety of things, so I’m not easily moved to try them. But I heard this decompresses the spine and trains your musculature to work properly as a functional unit.
I tried Eric’s Founder pose and, wow, it’s great. Not just because it feels good while you do it but your posture improves. And it definitely made me more flexible.

So what is it? It’s similar to the “chair pose” in yoga but while that mainly emphasizes the musculature of the front of the body, the Founder pose emphasizes mobility of your posterior and lateral chains: your hamstrings, glutes, lower and upper back, and thoracic muscles.
Here is how you do it: Stand with your feet a bit wider than your shoulders, toes pointing slightly out.
Stand as tall as you can by pressing your heels down and lifting your head up, as if a string were tied to the top of your head but your heels were fastened down to the ground.

Hinge your hips so you lean slightly forward at the waist—almost as though you’re about to sit in a chair but freeze only about a third of the way down into the movement. Your hips and glutes are back behind your heels, and your knees are just slightly bent. Keep your head as far away from your glutes as possible. You should feel a stretch in your lower back and hamstrings. If not, lean farther forward at the waist until you do.
Raise your chest, and with your arms at your sides, turn your thumbs out and away from the midline of your body (away from your belly button).
Keeping your thumbs rotated out, start to slowly lift your arms. Stop when you feel more stretching in your lower back and/or the backs of your legs.
Now move your hips back a few inches more. And raise your chest and head, aka “make your spine long,” still pressing your heels down.
Raise your arms a bit more if you can (thumbs still pointed away from your navel in external rotation), all the while pushing your heels down.
Hold this position for five more seconds then stand up straight.
Repeat that one to two times, as often as every day or even just a few times a week.
